entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders-london.txt" target="_blank">Agentic coding: A roundtable with industry leaders (London) - Speakers: Arnaud Giuliani (CPTO \& Co-founder @ Kotzilla), Christos Gkekas (Software Engineer), Iury Souza (Senior Engineer, SumUp), Maia Grotepass (Staff Engineer Android, Qonto), Slobodan Manojlović (VP, Lead Software Engineer), Tristan Hamilton (Technical Lead, HubSpot), Jose Alcérreca (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iQ0R0EfOBiw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders-london ## About the talk As new tools rapidly reshape modern software engineering, this panel will explore how companies and developers are leveraging agentic coding, automated agents, and specialized developer tooling in their daily workflows. We aim to highlight practical applications, discuss measurable productivity improvements, and candidly address the challenges engineering teams face when integrating these tools at scale. ## Summary - Code generation shifts development bottlenecks across the pipeline. Once teams accelerate code reviews, new constraints emerge around live experiments and safe production releases. - Specialized agent teams can replace single general assistants across complex domains. Teams build distinct agents for areas such as performance or logging, coordinating them through routers or shared pools. - Autonomous pull requests require guardrails and clear human accountability. Some workflows auto-submit routine fixes for tech debt, but each PR points back to a designated owner and relies on strict automated checks. - Harness engineering needs centralized shared tooling alongside room for experimentation. Teams maintain core infrastructure for shared concerns such as logs and crashes while pruning inactive skills through automated scripts. - Local developer hardware is strained by concurrent agent-driven builds. Engineers encounter exhausted memory and slow machines when agents trigger multiple Gradle builds simultaneously. ## Topics agentic-coding, ai-tooling, code-review, harness-engineering, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/actionable-strategies-for-reducing-your-apps-bitmap-memory-footprint.txt" target="_blank">Actionable strategies for reducing your app's Bitmap memory footprint - Speakers: Fung Lam (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KD_55WdEYj0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/actionable-strategies-for-reducing-your-apps-bitmap-memory-footprint ## About the talk Managing Bitmap memory is critical for mitigating Out-Of-Memory (OOM) risks in visually rich Android apps. While developers know to reduce image sizes, achieving long-term app stability comes from mastering two other key pillars: Reuse and Recycle. This session delivers a practical playbook for optimizing memory performance using modern tools, open-source libraries like Glide and Coil, and system-level APIs. In this session, you will learn how to diagnose real-world memory regressions using Android Vitals, implement advanced caching (Reuse) patterns with Glide and Coil, and proactively release memory (Recycle) using the onTrimMemory callback. ## Summary - Google Play is introducing memory performance thresholds enforced in February 2027. Exceeding the 90th percentile limit directly impacts your app's health assessment and can reduce visibility on the Play Store. - Bitmaps expand by dimensions and color depth when decoded, making them the largest memory consumers in most apps. Just a few full-resolution images can take hundreds of megabytes. - Downsample images and decode only visible regions to reduce memory consumption. Request matching image dimensions via CDN or use APIs like \`BitmapRegionDecoder\` rather than loading oversized full-resolution images. - Multiple image loaders multiply default memory heap cache usage and duplicate stored Bitmaps. Standardize on one loader or set explicit memory budgets across existing loaders. - Release image memory when your app moves to the background by handling \`onTrimMemory\`. Stop background polling and animations in \`onStop\` to prevent background memory growth. ## Resources - \[Android memory documentation\](https://developer.android.com/memory) ## Topics entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders.txt" target="_blank">Agentic coding: A roundtable with industry leaders - Speakers: Luis Artola (Engineering Manager), Ty Smith (Principal Engineer), Vinay Gaba (Senior Engineering Manager, Databricks), Kaushik Gopal (Principal Software Engineer), Annyce Davis (Sr. Director of Engineering), Ben Trengrove (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=megAzvXTdrc - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders ## About the talk As AI tools rapidly reshape modern software engineering, this panel will explore how developers are leveraging AI-assisted coding, automated agents and specialized developer tooling in their daily workflows. We aim to highlight practical applications, discuss measurable productivity improvements and candidly address the challenges engineering teams face when integrating AI at scale. Moderated by Ben Trengrove, Google Developer Relations Engineer ## Summary - AI tools accelerate code writing and PR creation, but teams face friction in downstream stages like code review and business approvals. - Code reviews are shifting from manual line-by-line checks toward agent-assisted verification and intent reviews. - CI infrastructure faces severe compute scaling challenges from rising code volumes, prompting investments in remote build execution and caching with Bazel. - Enterprises manage AI token costs with usage limits and automated model routing. ## Topics agentic-coding, developer-productivity, code-review, ci-infrastructure, token-economics, software-development-lifecycle ## Transcript ### Introduction and panelist introductions entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-workflows-with-small-models.txt" target="_blank">Agentic coding workflows with small models - Speakers: Ian Ballantyne (Technical Member of Staff, Google DeepMind), Jose Alcérreca (Developer Relations Engineer), Zoe Lopez-Latorre (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sBWgIjWU6PI - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-workflows-with-small-models ## About the talk While large frontier models dominate the headlines, small language models (SLMs) like Gemma 4 offer low-latency, cost-effective, and fully offline intelligence to augment daily developer workflows. This talk explores practical patterns for integrating small models into Android development, from smart task routing to cost optimization, using Gemma 4 as our primary hands-on case study to demonstrate real-world use cases and how to configure developer tools and agentic workflows. ## Summary - Small language models offer zero marginal cost and offline access on local hardware. Frontier models cost 20 to 200 times more for the same workloads. - Quantization-aware training cuts memory footprints by 75% with less loss than post-training compression. Speculative decoding then speeds up predictable coding tasks up to 3x. - Evaluating small models requires testing the full stack rather than relying on Python leaderboards. Android Bench provides 100 PR-sized tasks reflecting actual Android development. - Android Bench tests show Gemma 4 solves over half of tasks with its full context window enabled. Long-horizon tasks remain out of reach. - Multi-model orchestration combines frontier and small models through techniques like task cascading and automatic routing. This preserves reliability while reducing token costs. ## Resources - \[Are we there yet? (AWTY) framework\](https://goo.gle/awty) - \[Android Bench\](https://developer.android.com/bench) ## Topics small-language-models, agentic-workflows, benchmarking, gemma, android-studio, evaluations entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-engineering-with-claude-code-and-android-cli.txt" target="_blank">Agentic engineering with Claude Code and Android CLI - Speakers: Steven Jenkins (Product Manager, Android Studio), Ben Trengrove (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mb9H43ia0kE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-engineering-with-claude-code-and-android-cli ## About the talk Stop copy-pasting into AI chat windows and start delegating to your agent. This practical, example-driven session shows you how to level up your agentic engineering using Claude Code and the Android CLI. We will walk through a complete workflow to automate complex development tasks and ship features faster. You will learn to: - Optimize the token efficiency of your harness using Android CLI, Skills, Hooks and MCP. - Offload and parallelize long-running tasks to subagents. - Set up continuous verification loops that stop early termination and run until tests pass. ## Summary - Android CLI gives coding agents shell access to Android tools such as emulators and Firebase Crashlytics. It sits in your shell space and works across agents. - Keep agent conversations to around 150,000 tokens to prevent context rot. Slice work into scoped issues and run Gradle in quiet mode to avoid long logs. - Keep \`AGENTS.md\` under 250 lines and reserve it for permanent rules such as architecture constraints. Letting an agent edit this file degrades performance and raises costs. - Deterministic hooks and context-specific skills manage agent actions better than sprawling files. Install only vetted skills or start with the base Android CLI skill. - Verification loops stop developers from acting as manual QA testers. Tier checks to run fast unit tests first and slow emulator runs last. ## Resources - \[Android CLI installation\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Agent modification study\](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.11988) - \[Android Bench\](https://developer.android.com/bench) ## Topics claude-code, android-cli, agentic-engineering, benchmarking, performance ## Transcript ### This session breaks down the compliance pathways for all developers, from large studios to hobbyists. We will outline the key requirements for publishing on Google Play and third-party app stores. The talk will feature a live demo of the new Limited Distribution accounts, showing how students and hobbyists can easily and safely share apps. By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand the 3 main developer verification paths. See the new Limited Distribution account flow live. Identify your specific next steps for compliance. ## Summary - Android developer verification links distributed apps to accountable legal entities to curb financial fraud and burner malware networks. Regional enforcement began across four markets before global enforcement expands next year. - Developers can register through Google Play Console or a dedicated Android Developer Console. Students and hobbyists can register packages for free to share across up to 50 associated devices. - The Android Developer Console API enables third-party stores and developers to programmatically automate app registrations and resolve package conflicts. The Android Developer Status API checks whether package names are registered. - Experienced users can sideload unregistered apps by enabling Advanced Flow in developer options. This path enforces a device reboot and a 24-hour countdown to disrupt social engineering scams. ## Resources - \[Developer Console Documentation\](https://developer.android.com/console) ## Topics entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/app-security-in-the-agentic-era.txt" target="_blank">App security in the agentic era - Speakers: Kristen O'Leary (Senior Developer Relations Engineer), Sabs (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/app-security-in-the-agentic-era ## About the talk This presentation explores the strategic shift from viewing AI as a generic coding assistant to leveraging it as a context-aware, automated security peer reviewer integrated directly into the Android development lifecycle. We discuss how specialized AI agents, connected to the Android toolchain via skills, can help improve app security. By bridging the gap between raw LLM capabilities and deep project context, this approach empowers development teams to maintain high-velocity feature delivery without compromising rigorous security and policy standards. ## Summary - Generic AI agents miss key context during audits, but Android security skills provide researcher-backed guidance. They check intent security and enforce permissions using project-specific build configurations. - The Play policy skill runs static analysis to catch compliance issues before submission. It can cross-reference code analysis against existing Play Store declarations. - The Play Integrity API evaluates app and device integrity at runtime. The Protected with Play dashboard unites integrity and distribution monitoring in one place. - Targeted APIs allow apps to protect user privacy without requesting broad permissions. Examples include the SMS Retriever API and the alpha Location Button library. ## Skills - \[Android CLI and Android skills\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Resources - \[Google Bug Hunters key stats\](https://bughunters.google.com/about/key-stats) - \[Play Integrity API\](https://goo.gle/play-integrity-api) - \[Advanced Protection Mode\](https://goo.gle/aapm) - \[Location Button\](https://goo.gle/location-button) - \[SMS Retriever API\](https://goo.gle/sms-retriever-api) ## Topics app-security, ai-agents, play-integrity-api, permissions, location-button, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/architecting-spatial-content-on-android-xr-with-unity.txt" target="_blank">Architecting Spatial Content on Android XR with Unity - Speakers: Levana Chen (Software Engineer), Jennifer Stanton (Senior Software Engineer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/architecting-spatial-content-on-android-xr-with-unity ## About the talk Discover how to anchor and persist 3D experiences in the real world using Unity and Android XR. This session covers the Spatial Entities framework, Cloud Anchors, and Geospatial APIs, demonstrating how to build context-aware apps that remember physical placements and sync multi-user spatial data across sessions. We will examine the architecture behind spatial entities, understand how to anchor digital assets to physical objects, surfaces, and geographic locations. You will walk away with practical Unity workflows for mapping spaces, persisting content across sessions, and creating shared, location-aware AR/XR experiences. ## Summary - AR Foundation provides a unified scripting API across XR platforms using OpenXR extensions. It lets you represent and query real-world features such as planes and meshes. - Persistent anchors stabilize digital content across sessions and device restarts. You can persist them with \`TrySaveAnchorAsync\` and reload them using serialized GUIDs. - The Spatial Entities framework replaces trackable extensions to provide cross-platform support and better performance for tracking items like bounding boxes and markers. - Manager components should be disabled until Android XR permissions are granted. This avoids subsystem initialization failures caused by restricted access to sensitive environment data. - The Geospatial API uses Google Cloud ARCore services and VPS to position content at real-world outdoor locations. ## Resources - \[Unity Roadmap\](https://unity.com/roadmap) - \[AR Foundation Samples\](https://github.com/unity-technologies/arfoundation-samples) - \[Android XR with Unity Documentation\](https://d.android.com/develop/xr/unity) ## Topics android-xr, unity, ar-foundation, openxr, spatial-entities, anchors, geospatial-api ## Transcript ### Introduction and AR entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/balancing-ultra-low-latency-and-cloud-economics-in-virtual-voice-agents.txt" target="_blank">Balancing ultra-low latency and cloud economics in virtual voice agents - Speakers: Devin Reimer (CEO) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/balancing-ultra-low-latency-and-cloud-economics-in-virtual-voice-agents ## About the talk Bringing conversational AI into immersive experiences opens up huge possibilities, yet there's a constant friction between low response latency and sustainable cloud costs. In this session, Devin Reimer (Founder \& CEO of AstroBeam) breaks down how the team behind Stellar Cafe achieved industry-leading voice interaction response times (1.15s--1.4s) while keeping the business model commercially sustainable. Explore the hybrid architecture behind these low latency pipelines, focusing on intelligent orchestration between on-device models and optimized cloud inference to cut expensive API calls without degrading dialogue. You'll walk away with a practical blueprint covering Time-to-First-Token optimization across Speech-to-Text and streaming Text-to-Speech pipelines, parallel safety guardrails that bypass latency overhead, and unit economics per active user session. ## Summary - End-to-end latency around 1.5 seconds lets conversational voice agents feel comfortable to users without slowness complaints. Consistency matters even more than peak speed so conversations never feel broken. - Parallelizing speech pipelines cuts response times and stays 3 to 5 times cheaper than speech-to-speech models. Running safety checks concurrently alongside initial text-to-speech chunks adds zero latency. - Agent intelligence demands low transcription error rates and expressive speech. Crucially, models must also remain easy to build with so developers avoid brittle engineering overhead. - Cloud economics must be modeled up front by comparing per-user server costs against expected revenue. Stellar Cafe achieved viable margins at about $1.20 per hour per user with flat pricing. - Open-weight models avoid the frequent sunsets and rising fees typical of closed models. Self-hosting them provides predictable costs and protects production schedules from forced migrations. ## Resources - \[Devin Reimer on Bluesky\](https://devinreimer.bsky.social) - \[AstroBeam website\](https://astrobeam.com) - \[Devin Reimer on LinkedIn\](https://linkedin.com/in/devinreimer) ## Topics voice-agents, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, large-language-models, low-latency, cloud-economics, game-development ## Transcript ### Introduction to voice agents and core challenges \*\*Devin Reimer\*\* \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=5s) Welcome to co-founder of Owlchemy Labs, probably most known for Job Simulator. \[00:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=23s) So, at AstroBeam, we are focused on building real-time AI in games. In this session, discover how Firebase AI Logic empowers developers to deploy secure, budget-conscious AI experiences at scale. We will cover from security foundations and Firebase App Check, cost management, dynamic model routing to leveraging the multimodal capabilities. ## Summary - Firebase AI Logic routes requests from client SDKs directly to Gemini APIs without a custom back end. Server prompt templates store prompts in the cloud to avoid app updates. - Firebase App Check protects resources against abuse by ensuring requests originate from your app. It integrates attestation providers like Play Integrity and reCAPTCHA Enterprise before you enforce checks. - Gemini Nano 4 executes on-device inference to lower latency and safeguard user privacy. Firebase AI Logic manages fallback routing to the cloud when needed. - Spend caps and Firebase AI Logic triggers keep cloud costs predictable. Firebase automatically pauses your AI service at 100% spend, and triggers let you run custom functions before or after generation. - Gemini Live API powers bidirectional conversational audio and video streaming. The client SDK manages the underlying WebSocket connections and streaming protocols. ## Topics firebase-ai-logic, gemini-nano, firebase-app-check, on-device-ai, cost-optimization, gemini-live-api ## entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/build-world-anchored-experiences-for-xreal-aura-wired-xr-glasses.txt" target="_blank">Build world anchored experiences for wired XR glasses - Speakers: Yasmine Quintana Evjen (Senior Product Manager), Dereck Bridie (Developer Relations Engineer), Paul Hoover (Senior Interaction Designer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/build-world-anchored-experiences-for-xreal-aura-wired-xr-glasses ## About the talk Go beyond screen-space and anchor your apps in the real world with Android XR. This session teaches you how to build geospatially aware Android XR experiences using Jetpack Compose Glimmer and ARCore's Geospatial API. We will start by covering how to get a device's geospatial pose with ARCore. Then, you'll see how Glimmer's minimal UI components can be anchored to real-world locations via the Visual Positioning System (VPS). We'll combine these to build a simple, location-aware spatial experience. ## Summary - Android XR brings digital experiences into physical environments across a spectrum of devices, from intelligent eyewear to wired XR glasses. Existing 2D Android-compatible apps work on XR headsets and wired XR glasses with minimal modifications. - Jetpack Compose Glimmer provides components and styles tailored for optical see-through displays. Built-in helper functions adjust brand colors to glasses-safe shades to maintain visibility and contrast across lighting conditions. - The Glimmer library adds new components such as pagers and button groups. A depth API helps separate stacked elements on see-through displays where black is transparent. - Subspace composables place interfaces in 3D space and can follow ARCore anchors via a follow target, such as a tracked QR code. - The Geospatial API in ARCore combines Street View data and GPS measurements to position devices accurately in supported areas. You can attach Glimmer components to real-world geospatial anchors using coordinates from Places API queries. ## Resources - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Glimmer guide\](https://goo.gle/glimmer-guide) - \[Geospatial API documentation\](https://goo.gle/xr-geospatial) - \[Android XR developer resources\](https://goo.gle/xr-dev) - \[Android XR experiments\](https://goo.gle/xr-experiments) - \[Android XR codelabs\](https://goo.gle/xr-codelabs) - \[Android XR developer documentation\](https://developer.android.com/xr) ## Topics android-xr, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-a-formula-e-co-driver-on-android-with-ml-kit-and-gemini-nano.txt" target="_blank">Building a Formula E co-driver on Android with ML Kit and Gemini Nano - Speakers: Alastair Breeze (Staff Software Engineer - Google Cloud's Office of the CTO), Oli Thompson (Junior Data Scientist, Formula E) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nV63eqjPeEI - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-a-formula-e-co-driver-on-android-with-ml-kit-and-gemini-nano ## About the talk A racing car is a demanding environment of high speed, heat, and telemetry constraints. How can an on-device agent help process real-time vehicle data for sports and engineering applications? This technical session explores an experimental hybrid architecture combining edge hardware and cloud agents. We'll walk through a research proof-of-concept using a Raspberry Pi to stream CAN bus telemetry, a Pixel phone running an on-device conversational agent powered by ML Kit and Gemini Nano, and an agent-to-agent (A2A) Cloud connection for post-race workflows. ## Summary - Formula E race environments challenge edge AI with extreme heat and low latency requirements. A Pixel phone hosted an agent to answer drivers traveling over 200 km/h. - Android hosts the edge architecture using Agent Developer Kit and Gemini Nano through ML Kit. Edge agents can converse directly with cloud agents over the A2A protocol. - Vehicle integration routes live CAN bus telemetry through a Raspberry Pi to publish downsampled 10 Hz data over MQTT. The Android agent combines this data with driver voice input to evaluate queries and speak back. - Track testing at Goodwood proved the phone handled severe heat without issues. Last-minute debugging resolved Bluetooth connections to the driver helmet before the car drove up the hill. ## Topics gemini-nano, ml-kit, on-device-ai, ai-agents, formula-e ## Transcript ### entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-audio-first-experiences-for-intelligent-eyewear-with-gemini-nano-4.txt" target="_blank">Building audio-first experiences for intelligent eyewear with Gemini Nano 4 - Speakers: Amy Zeppenfeld (Developer Relations Engineer \| Android XR), Alice Zheng (Senior Product Manager) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-audio-first-experiences-for-intelligent-eyewear-with-gemini-nano-4 ## About the talk Discover how to build robust, hands-free audio experiences powered by on-device AI. We'll cover everything you need: setting up your glasses activity, capturing mic and camera feeds, and using voice along with other audio cues as your ultimate UI. Through an exciting real-world showcase of the open-source XR Language Teacher built in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, learn to orchestrate Gemini Nano 4 (built on Gemma 4 and optimized for Android devices), and ML Kit, and leverage the LiteRT runtime to build fast XR experiences that hear, see, and speak naturally. ## Summary - The Jetpack Projected library (alpha) bridges Android phones to intelligent eyewear. Adding a projected activity to your existing app projects content to display or audio-only glasses. - ML Kit introduces alpha on-device speech libraries for audio-first interactions on select devices. It offers Text to Speech with 8 voices across 21 locales and Speech Recognition with a Gemini Nano advanced mode on Pixel 10. - Gemini Nano 4 processes camera frames and transcribed questions together in one pass. It powers offline experiences by chaining on-device speech models locally on supported flagship phones. - A two-pass design prioritizes real-time audio latency on smart glasses. Pass 1 streams spoken text using inline XML tags for mid-sentence locale switching, while Pass 2 extracts structured data in the background. - The open-source XR Language Teacher implementation ships in the Google AI Edge Gallery app. Developers can adapt its code for other multimodal assistant use cases. ## Resources - \[Android XR Developer Documentation\](https://goo.gle/xr-dev) - \[Android XR SDK and Developer Resources\](https://developer.android.com/xr) - \[ML Kit APIs Documentation\](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit) - \[Google AI Edge Offerings and Gallery App\](https://developers.google.com/edge) - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Topics intelligent-eyewear, android-xr, gemini-nano, on-device-ai, ml-kit, speech-recognition, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-reliable-text-editing-experiences-in-compose.txt" target="_blank">Building reliable text editing experiences in Compose - Speakers: Anastasia Soboleva (Software engineer), Haoyu Zhang (Senior Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-reliable-text-editing-experiences-in-compose ## About the talk The journey to reliable text editing in Compose culminated in the complete rewrite of BasicTextField. This shift to a buffer-driven architecture eliminated IME race conditions once and for all. This session unpacks why legacy input syncing had to go and how TextFieldState keeps keyboard updates in sync. From there, take a deep dive into formatted editing to explore the mechanics of TrackedRange, the performance costs of edit blocks, and the real-world catches behind style boundaries, before taking an early peek at Markdown rendering. ## Summary - The \`TextFieldState\` API overload replaces the callback-based overloads in Compose. It updates synchronously with user typing, eliminating timing issues with software keyboards and unnecessary recompositions. - Input and output transformations let you manipulate text using \`TextFieldBuffer\`. You can intercept edits before committing them or format display text without manually computing offset mappings. - Hoisting \`TextFieldState\` depends on your architecture needs. You can keep it locally in a composable or store it directly in a \`ViewModel\` for business logic access. - Compose 1.12 adds formatted text editing APIs to \`TextFieldBuffer\`. You can apply styles with customizable \`ExpandPolicy\` options, and existing style ranges update automatically as users edit. - A new markup text library for Jetpack Compose is currently in development. It supports formats like Markdown with incremental parsing and rendering for live editing and streaming. ## Resources - \[Migration guide to TextFieldState\](https://goo.gle/migrate_to_state_textfield) ## Topics jetpack-compose, textfieldstate, text-editing, basictextfield, formatted-text, input-transformation ## Transcript ### Introduction to text editing in Compose \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=5s) Hi, everyone! \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=6s) Thank you for joining our talk. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=8s) My name is Anastasia, and with me is my colleague Haoyu. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=11s) And we are going to show you today how to build reliable text-editing experience. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=16s) Whether you are building a simple login screen, a search as you type bar, or a complex messaging app, text fields are at the heart of how users interact with your Android apps. \[00:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=29s) So, most of you probably already use material text fields, or outlined text fields. \`\`\`kotlin TextField(state = rememberTextFieldState()) \`\`\` \`\`\`kotlin OutlinedTextField(state = rememberTextFieldState()) \`\`\` \[00:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=34s) There is also a \`BasicTextField\` for if you are building an on your own design system, or you need a simple editing box. \`\`\`kotlin BasicTextField(state = rememberTextFieldState()) \`\`\` \[00:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=44s) There is also \`SecureTextField\` which is specifically designed to enter passwords. \`\`\`kotlin SecureTextField(state = rememberTextFieldState()) \`\`\` \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=50s) And \`BasicTextField\` is an unstyled component and is actually powers all of other text fields in Compose. \[00:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=58s) So, you might have noticed over the past few years that we have two API shapes in parallel, one taking value and value change call back, and the other one taking \`TextFieldState\` object. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable public fun BasicTextField( state: TextFieldState, ) \`\`\` \[01:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=68s) So, you might wonder which one we recommend. \[01:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=72s) We strongly encourage using the \`TextFieldState\` overload. \[01:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=76s) And we will discuss in this talk why it's the its benefits in terms of API, features, and performance. \[01:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=84s) It has been stable since Compose 1.7. \[01:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=88s) As for the call back overloads, we are soft-deprecating them in Compose 1.13 across \`BasicTextField\` and material wrappers. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable public fun BasicTextField( value: String, onValueChange: (String) -\> Unit ) @Composable public fun BasicTextField( value: TextFieldValue, onValueChange: (TextFieldValue) -\> Unit \`\`\` \[01:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=97s) It means that we are not going to add any new features or fixing bugs unless you know, critical security issues or accessibility. \[01:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=108s) The stateless value on value change overload was really really worked well for synchronous inputs. \[01:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=116s) But as soon as you paired it with asynchronous streams, for instance, \`StateFlow\`, it created timing issues with the IME or as technical term, for the software keyboard. \[02:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=127s) So, that caused dropped characters, duplicated characters, cursor jumps, as you can see on this recording. ### Introducing TextFieldState \[02:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=135s) To fix this fundamentally, we introduced \`TextFieldState\`. \[02:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=139s) It updates synchronously when the user types without waiting for those async round trips, which is exactly what the IME needed. \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=148s) \`TextFieldState\`, in addition to the read-only text, also has other properties that kind of create a active editing session. \[02:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=159s) That is selection, undo redo state, and also span and span styles and paragraph styles for formatted text editing, more on that later in this talk. \[02:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=170s) The internal properties of the \`TextFieldState\` are backed by the Compose Snapshot System. \[02:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=174s) So, it means when you read those text or selection from that \`TextFieldState\` object somewhere in Compose, the specific scope where you read it from is subscribed to the updates. \[03:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=186s) It allows \`BasicTextField\` to only read state in the layout or draw phases, and together with some it eliminates the unnecessary recomposition when the user types. \[03:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=197s) And together with some other changes, it delivered a significant performance improvement for the \`TextFieldState\` overload. \[03:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=205s) Now, if the TextFieldState's text is a read-only property, how do you actually make programmatic changes to your input field? \[03:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=213s) And this is where the TextFieldBuffer comes in handy. \[03:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=216s) It's a mutable object that gives you APIs to make changes. \[03:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=222s) So, when you want to make the programmatic change, you call the edit function of the \`TextFieldState\`. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=228s) And inside that lambda, you get a TextFieldBuffer. \[03:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=231s) And TextFieldBuffer exposes several functions that allow you to insert, replace characters, delete them as required. \[04:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=241s) One quick tip with the edit is that avoid calling them multiple times in a row. \`\`\`kotlin // Often generated by AI agents: state.edit { insert(5, ",") } state.edit { delete(12, 13) } state.edit { replace(0, 5, "goodbye") } state.edit { selection = TextRange(9, 16) } \`\`\` \[04:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=249s) Instead, batch all of your operations into a single edit call. \`\`\`kotlin // Batch all operations in a single atomic edit: state.edit { insert(5, ",") delete(12, 13) replace(0, 5, "goodbye") selection = TextRange(9, 16) } \`\`\` \[04:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=253s) In that way, Compose will only create a single instance of the TextFieldBuffer, mutates it in place, and then synchronize it with the IME and Snapshot System once. \[04:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=265s) Another tip is that for most common batch operations that you will need, we actually have extension extension functions on the \`TextFieldState\`. \`\`\`kotlin fun TextFieldState.setTextAndPlaceCursorAtEnd(text: String) { edit { replace(0, length, text) placeCursorAtEnd() } } \`\`\` \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=274s) So, you don't need to think about batching those operations. \[04:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=277s) You just call one of those. \[04:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=278s) An example would be \`clearText\` and \`setTextAndPlaceCursorAtEnd\`. \`\`\`kotlin fun TextFieldState.clearText() { edit { delete(0, length) placeCursorAtEnd() } } \`\`\` ### Input filtering and formatting \[04:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=285s) So, now what about filtering the user input? \[04:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=289s) Like, enforcing a character limit or wanting to accept digits only. \[04:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=295s) In the old API, filtering in the \`onValueChange\` ran after the text was already committed. \`\`\`kotlin onValueChange { newString -\> // full diffing new String vs old String } \`\`\` \[05:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=301s) And so, rejecting or altering that input kind of fought with the keyboard. \[05:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=307s) Also, the \`onValueChange\` callback only gave you the final string. \[05:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=312s) So to understand what changed, you had to do the full-string diffing. \[05:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=317s) Instead, in the new overload, we have input transformation. \`\`\`kotlin @Stable public fun interface InputTransformation { public fun TextFieldBuffer.transformInput() } \`\`\` \[05:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=321s) So it intercepts user input before that input reaches the text field state, and it give you gives you that same TextFieldBuffer APIs. \[05:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=333s) So this is how you implement the digits-only filtering with the input transformation, and you basically just take the change it take the changes. \`\`\`kotlin // Intercept and filter input during typing inputTransformation = InputTransformation { val text = asCharSequence() if (!text.all { it.isDigit() }) { // Reject non-digit characters revertAllChanges() } } \`\`\` \[05:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=340s) You check if there is non-digits characters, and then if there are, you reject the input by calling \`revertAllChanges\` on that TextFieldBuffer. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=350s) And the key capability of this input transformation is ChangeList. \[05:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=354s) So instead of diffing the full strings, it allows you to inspect the exact edit ranges, and then mutate them in place or reject the input altogether if needed. \[06:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=366s) And Compose will keep the keyboard and cursor in sync automatically for you. \[06:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=374s) Finally, what if you want to do visual formatting of your input? \[06:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=379s) For example, you want to add parentheses or dashes into a credit card number or phone number. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=386s) Oh, yeah. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=386s) And you don't want to take to store those in your database, right? \[06:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=390s) So previously, you used visual transformation API. \[06:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=394s) So in that case, you had to implement a bi-directional mapping from the raw input to the visual output, and then back. \[06:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=401s) And it was really difficult to make it right, which often led to runtime exceptions. \[06:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=408s) Now we have an output transformation, and then, again, under the hood, it is powered by the same TextFieldBuffer, so you get the same API pretty much. \`\`\`kotlin @Stable public fun interface OutputTransformation { public fun TextFieldBuffer.transformOutput() } \`\`\` \[06:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=418s) So in this phone number example, you simply, to insert those dash- dashes on a specific index, you simply call insert function of the TextFieldBuffer, and the system will calculate the bidirectional offset mapping for you. \`\`\`kotlin // Raw data untouched; formatting is purely visual outputTransformation = OutputTransformation { if (length \> 6) { insert(6, "-") } if (length \> 3) { insert(3, "-") } } \`\`\` \[07:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=435s) So this eliminates manual math and decreases the amount of crashes significantly. ### Hoisting and migrating TextFieldState \[07:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=444s) Now to the most important part, how do you actually migrate, and where do you hoist that \`TextFieldState\`? \[07:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=453s) In practice, almost every use case falls into one of those categories that I'm going to talk. \[07:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=459s) And when it is not, it Well, usually it means that you have some unconventional architecture, but these examples are still will still g- guide you through your migration. \[07:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=471s) Okay, so the simplest case is to keep the \`TextFieldState\` right inside your composable where that text field lives. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun PromoCodeInput(onApply: (String) -\> Unit) { // State hoisted locally inside the composable val state = rememberTextFieldState() OutlinedTextField( state = state, inputTransformation = InputTransformation.maxLength(6).allCaps(Locale.current), trailingIcon = { Button(onClick = { onApply(state.text.toString()) }) { } ) } \`\`\` \[08:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=480s) This is when the your text field is a self-contained input field, so, for instance, a promo code input field, and you only need to get access to that text when the user, for instance, submits presses the submit button, right? \[08:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=495s) And so your view model doesn't need to intercept the user input on every change. \[08:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=501s) So you just call \`rememberTextFieldState\` locally, and \`rememberTextFieldState\` also helps you with the state restoration after the process death. \[08:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=512s) Then you use input transformation for filtering, and you get the text from that state, TextFieldState object, and when the user submits, and you pass it through the lambda. \[08:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=527s) Okay, what if sibling UI elements like a character counter or a submit button also need to read the text or change it, make changes to it? \[08:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=538s) This brings us to a case where you hoist the \`TextFieldState\` object up to a common composable function, a common ancestor composable function. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun PostCommentBar(onSubmit: (String) -\> Unit) { // to share between UI components val commentState = rememberTextFieldState() Column { CommentTextField(commentState) Row { Text("${commentState.text.length} / 280") SubmitButton(commentState) } } \`\`\` \[09:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=548s) And because \`TextFieldState\` is backed by the snapshot system, passing it through the ancestor doesn't trigger recomposition of the parents. \[09:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=557s) Only those places where you actually read the state's text will update. \[09:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=566s) Okay. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=567s) So for complex UI use cases where you need your \`TextFieldState\`, input and output transformation to coordinate state internally, instead of hoisting them separately and trying to wire them together in the composable function, use a state holder object. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun PostEditor() { // Hoisting and wiring related pieces separately in the composable val textFieldState = rememberTextFieldState() val tagRanges = remember { mutableStateListOf() } val entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-type-safe-deep-links-with-jetpack-navigation3.txt" target="_blank">Building type-safe deep links with Jetpack Navigation3 - Speakers: Clara Fok (Software Engineer), Ian Lake (Engineering Manager) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-type-safe-deep-links-with-jetpack-navigation3 ## About the talk Managing deep links across modular Android apps can easily lead to broken routes and runtime surprises.This session unpacks Jetpack Navigation3's new type-safe deep linking architecture for Compose to help you build a robust and scalable routing system. We'll explore how to implement out-of-the-box deep link matching APIs, write custom serializers for complex type-safe arguments, and construct dynamic hierarchical back stacks that keep user navigation predictable. ## Summary - Navigation 3 deep link APIs turn incoming deep link requests into navigation keys to determine your initial back stack. The KMP-compatible \`DeepLinkRequest\` class encapsulates the input, including an Android Intent constructor. - A \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` uses Kotlin Serialization to match URI patterns and deserialize arguments into type-safe \`NavKey\` properties. Primitive types work automatically, failing matches if values cannot be parsed. - Developers can extend \`DeepLinkSerializer\` or override \`matchArguments\` to handle complex deep link strings. Subclassing \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` lets you preprocess raw URI placeholders before Kotlin Serialization runs. - Calling \`withBackStack\` on matchers creates synthetic back stacks lazily for the best match. This ensures proper system back behavior without computing unnecessary back stacks for every other valid match. ## Resources - \[Nav3 recipes repository\](https://goo.gle/nav3-recipes) - \[Now in Android sample app\](https://github.com/android/nowinandroid) ## Topics jetpack-navigation-3, deep-links, kotlin-serialization, kotlin-multiplatform, android-architecture ## Transcript ### \[00:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=9s) And I'm Clara Fok, the tech lead for Nav 3. \[00:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=12s) And today, we're here to talk to Nav2 and Nav3 as part of Nav3's 1.2 release. \[00:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=24s) I think you actually did it three times, cuz we also did an implementation in the Nav 3 recipes, as well. \[00:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=30s) Yes, that is true. \[00:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=31s) We went through a lot of iteration on both the recipes and our final APIs are very similar, because in Nav 3, you own the Back Stack. \[03:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=207s) That means that focus of our deep link APIs is to figure out what that initial Back Stack should be, specifically what screen do your users see when they click on a deep link to enter your app. \[03:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=218s) But what actually happens when the user clicks on that web URI? \[03:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=222s) Now, Now, where it gets interesting is what happens once that deep link triggers your Activity to start. \[03:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=236s) Here, the input is the Intent that your app is started with, that Activity that started. \[04:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=243s) But the deep link can take many forms. \[04:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=245s) For example, you may want to construct it manually for a test, or you may want to take advantage of your Kotlin Multiplatform support. \[04:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=253s) So, we've encapsulated the deep link input into a KMP-compatible \`DeepLinkRequest\` class. \[04:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=259s) And on Android, we have a \`DeepLinkRequest\` constructor that takes in an Android Intent. \[04:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=265s) Next, our goal is to figure out, given a request, how do we know what \`NavKey\` needs to be put on your Back Stack? \[04:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=271s) This is where our \`DeepLinkMatcher\` class comes in. \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=274s) It takes in a request and outputs a \`MatchResult\`, which contains the \`NavKey\` associated with the match. \[04:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=281s) Specifically for web URIs, we have a \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` that encapsulates all the logic needed to transform a given request into a \`MatchResult\`. \`\`\`kotlin val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( ..., ... ) \`\`\` \[04:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=293s) Now, the first parameter that a \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` takes is a URI pattern. \`\`\`kotlin val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri(...), ... ) \`\`\` \[04:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=298s) So, let's say you were building an ADS app, and you want to add a deep link to the home screen. \[05:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=304s) Here, the pattern is an exact URI, and we can leave out the HTTP schema to automatically match both HTTP and HTTPS. \`\`\`kotlin val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("ads.android.com/home"), ... ) \`\`\` \[05:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=312s) But if we wanted to deep link to a particular ADS session, now that deep link contains information that we need to extract, namely the session ID. \`\`\`kotlin // target NavKey @Serializable data class Session(val id: String) : NavKey val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("ads.android.com/session/{id}"), ... ) \`\`\` \[05:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=322s) So in this case, our pattern uses curly braces to act as placeholders for information that we need to extract from the deep link. \[05:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=331s) And it turns out there's already a handy library to convert any kind of input into class instances, which is Kotlin Serialization. \[05:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=339s) So our \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` leverages a Kotlin decoder to deserialize an input URI and output a \`NavKey\` instance. \`\`\`kotlin // target NavKey @Serializable data class Session(val id: String) : NavKey val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("ads.android.com/session/{id}"), serializer = serializer() ) \`\`\` \[05:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=348s) Now, that decoder needs to know what class to work with, so you'll also need to pass in a serializer for your \`NavKey\` into the matcher. \`\`\`kotlin // target NavKey @Serializable data class Session(val id: String) : NavKey val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("http://ads.android.com/session/{id}"), serializer = serializer() ) \`\`\` \[05:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=357s) And to help the decoder properly match match placeholders to the key's properties, the placeholder's name must match the property names. \[06:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=366s) So in this example, the property name is ID matching the session's ID parameter. \[06:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=372s) Okay, now that we have our \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\`, we need to construct a \`DeepLinkRequest\` with the incoming deep link. \`\`\`kotlin // target NavKey @Serializable data class Session(val id: String) : NavKey val matcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("http://ads.android.com/session/{id}"), serializer = serializer() ) val request = DeepLinkRequest( uri = DeepLinkUri("http://ads.android.com/session/abcd") ) val matchResult: UriMatchResult? = matcher.match(request) val backStack = listOf(matchResult?.key ?: Home) \`\`\` \[06:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=379s) Then matching is done by calling the match function, passing in our request. \[06:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=384s) This will give you a nullable \`MatchResult\` containing the \`NavKey\`, which in our example would be the session key, or if the result is null, we can just default to the home screen. \[06:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=397s) Now, multiple deep links should be written as multiple matchers: one matcher for each deep link. \[06:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=403s) So for example, here we have two URI patterns for our session key: one for a legacy newsletter pattern and one for a regular web URI. \[06:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=412s) And we also have a deep link to the ADS home screen, so we add a third matcher for that. \[06:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=417s) And all the matchers would be added to the same list that we iterate through. \[07:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=421s) So now our match becomes a loop over all the matchers in our list, where we call match on each one to find all the matchers that matches the request. \[07:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=431s) To do that, we could use \`mapNotNull\` to filter out the non-matches and get back a list of only the valid matches. \`\`\`kotlin val matchers = listOf(...) // gets all non-null MatchResult val matchResults = matchers.mapNotNull { matcher -\> matcher.match(request) } \`\`\` \[07:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=439s) Now in most cases, you'll probably only have one non-null match in your list, but there are cases where there can be more than one valid match. \[07:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=447s) For example, let's say we introduce a special keynote screen reusing the same session URI pattern, but now instead of the ID placeholder, it has a static keynote path. \[07:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=458s) So in this case, the same request can match both matchers: the session key where the ID equals keynote and the keynote \`NavKey\`. \[07:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=468s) So since \`MatchResult\` implements Comparable, we can find the best match by comparing all of the valid matches in the list using the max function, or really \`maxOrNull\` to handle the case where there weren't any deep links matching the request. \`\`\`kotlin val matchers = listOf(...) // gets all non-null MatchResult val matchResults = matchers.mapNotNull { matcher -\> matcher.match(request) } // compare matches val backStack = listOf( matchResults.maxOrNull()?.key ?: Home ) \`\`\` \[08:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=484s) Now, a static list of matchers might make sense for a lightning talk, but just like how your screens can be spread across multiple modules, we expect those same modules to contribute to a global list of matchers via your DI system. \`\`\`kotlin // Feature A Module @ContributesTo(ActivityScope::class) @BindingContainer object FeatureAModule { @IntoSet @Provides fun provideDeepLinkMatcher() : UriDeepLinkMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern = DeepLinkUri("ads.android.com/featureA"), serializer(), ) } // in MainActivity @Inject lateinit var matchers: Set\> \`\`\` \[08:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=497s) And using this approach, our Hilt, Metro, and Koin recipes in our recipes repo have been updated to include deep links. ### Type-safe deserialization and custom serializers \[08:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=510s) Now, Clara mentioned that our \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` uses Kotlin Serialization to extract fields out of the deep link request and make it into our type-safe class, like our session class we showed. \[08:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=522s) As written here, this is a pretty simple transformation. \[08:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=525s) The URI is a string. \[08:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=527s) The field's a string. \[08:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=528s) Wow, that was easy. \[08:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=529s) But we know that we needed to go beyond just string properties. \[08:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=534s) This is where Kotlin Serialization already gives us a solid foundation to work with. \[08:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=539s) All the primitive types, like Booleans, integers, floats, even Enums work out of the box, automatically failing the match and returning null if the deep link value can't be parsed as that specific type. \[09:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=555s) For example, if our session's ID parameter were actually an integer instead of a string, passing in a string that couldn't be parsed in integer would fail the match. \`\`\`kotlin // pattern = "http://ads.android.com/session/{id}" @Serializable data class Session(val id: Int) : NavKey \`\`\` \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=567s) Similarly, if you wanted to have optional arguments, say for analytics data attached to your web URL, those could be properties on your key that have default values. \`\`\`kotlin // pattern = "http://ads.android.com/session/{id}#referrer={referrer} @Serializable data class Session( val id: Int, val referrer: String? = null, ) : NavKey from the type-safe classes or classes that represent the deep link match in your app. \[09:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=593s) Because I know some of you are handling some absolutely terrible deep links. \`\`\`kotlin // "id={id}\&base64={placeholderImage}" @Serializable data class Session( val id: String, val placeholderImage: Bitmap? = null ) : NavKey // "jsonBlob={user}" @Serializable data class Profile( val user: User, ) : NavKey \`\`\` \[09:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=598s) You know, maybe you have a base64 encoded image attached to your deep link. \[10:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=603s) You know, maybe a giant JSON blob that they decided, "Oh, let's just put that into every URL of your app." transformed from a String into your type-safe property. \`\`\`kotlin object BitmapSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer() { ... } \`\`\` \[10:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=632s) The \`DeepLinkSerializer\` is a helper wrapper around Kotlin Serialization that simplifies implementing their serializer class, because in this case, the deserializer input is just always a String from your web URL. \`\`\`kotlin public abstract class DeepLinkSerializer : KSerializer \`\`\` \[10:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=647s) Now to implement a \`DeepLinkSerializer\`, you write three methods. \[10:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=651s) First, you choose a serial name. \`\`\`kotlin object BitmapSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer() { override val serialName: String get() = "Bitmap" ... } \`\`\` \[10:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=653s) Doesn't need to be namespaced, but it needs to be unique enough that Kotlin Serialization knows when to use your serializer. \[11:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=661s) Next, you need to implement deserialize, which is passed that String from your web URL and is responsible for constructing your type-safe object. \`\`\`kotlin object BitmapSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer() { override val serialName: String get() = "Bitmap" override fun to the property that has that class that's a little special, and web \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` will take care of the rest. \`\`\`kotlin object BitmapSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer() { ... } @Serializable data class Session( val id: String, @Serializable(BitmapSerializer::class) val placeholderImage: Bitmap? = null ) : NavKey \`\`\` ### Preprocessing URL arguments with custom matchers \[11:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=696s) But what if you only want a little bit of the data from that base 64 String, or that JSON that was attached to your web URL? \[11:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=705s) In that case, it might make sense to pre-process some of your web URL before it gets to Kotlin Serialization at all. \[11:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=714s) To handle those cases, you can extend \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` and override its \`matchArguments\` method. \[12:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=722s) Now, maybe for our JSON blob, all we really want is just that session ID, like we actually don't care about any of the rest of that. UriDeepLinkMatcher(uriPattern, serializer=serializer()) { override fun matchArguments( pathArgs: Map\>, queryArgs: Map\>, fragmentArgs: Map\> ): UriMatchResult? { ... } \`\`\` \[12:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=733s) The inputs are those raw strings, all the place holders that were added from your URI path. \[12:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=741s) And that allows us to pre-process and edit those values before we call into \`super.matchArguments\`. \`\`\`kotlin class SessionUriDeepLinkMatcher( uriPattern: DeepLinkUri ) : UriDeepLinkMatcher(uriPattern, serializer=serializer()) { override fun matchArguments( pathArgs: Map\>, queryArgs: Map\>, fragmentArgs: Map\> ): UriMatchResult? { val finalQueryArgs = buildMap { putAll(queryArgs) val jsonBlob = remove("session")?.firstOrNull() if (jsonBlob != null) { put("session", extractSessionIdFromJson(jsonBlob)) } } return super.matchArguments(pathArgs, finalQueryArgs, fragmentArgs) } \`\`\` \[12:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=750s) Now, we can have simplified values here, and we don't need to mess with Kotlin Serialization at all. ### Building synthetic back stacks for deep links \[12:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=759s) Thanks, Ian. \[12:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=762s) Hopefully you won't have to reach out to those techniques often, but we did put a lot of thought into how you can control the matching behavior. \[12:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=770s) Okay. \[12:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=770s) Now that we know how to get a \`NavKey\` with the deep link matchers, but a back stack with only the navigation key may not provide the best user experience. \[12:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=779s) So, to ensure the proper back behavior, you'd want a synthetic back stack. \[13:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=783s) The synthetic part comes from the fact that the back stack contains keys that the user never manually navigated to, but it is the path that they would have taken if they did manually navigate there. \[13:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=794s) So, for example, clicking on a notification for a session that's about to start, you'd take the user directly to that session, but when they trigger system back, you'd probably want them to go back to your HomeScreen before exiting to the launcher. \[13:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=808s) That HomeScreen becomes part of the Synthetic Back Stack. \[13:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=812s) Now for deep link APIs, we wanted to compete we wanted to balance two competing requirements. \[13:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=819s) On the one side, we know that different deep links, or different matchers, would want different logic for building their synthetic back stack. \[13:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=826s) So for example, adding a HomeScreen before every deep link might work until you want to deep link to a sub-screen inside a setting screen. \[13:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=834s) Now, you need an extra layer in your synthetic back stack for that particular deep link. \[13:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=839s) Naturally, this ties the back stack builder to each deep link matcher. \[14:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=843s) But on the other hand, we also know that every millisecond leading up to the correct screen being displayed costs you all real money. \[14:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=850s) So we didn't want to compute a synthetic back stack for every match result. \[14:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=854s) We wanted just for the best match. \[14:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=857s) So, if we want custom logic for each matcher, but we don't want to create a synthetic back stack eagerly for each match, what do we do? \[14:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=866s) So after a few false starts, we found an approach that balances both requirements. \[14:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=871s) No matter what kind of matcher you have, you can augment that specific matcher by calling a \`withBackStack\` to lazily construct the back stack with the given \`MatchResult\`. \`\`\`kotlin val homeMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher(...).withBackStack { matchResult -\> listOf(Home, matchResult.key) } val sessionMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher(...).withBackStack { matchResult -\> listOf(Home, SessionList, matchResult.key) } val backStackMatchers: List\> = listOf( homeMatcher, sessionMatcher ) val matchResults = backStackMatchers.mapNotNull { matcher.match(request) } val bestMatch: BackStackMatchResult? = matchResults.maxOrNull() val backStack = bestMatch?.backStack ?: listOf(Home) \`\`\` \[14:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=882s) So, if we have multiple matchers, each one would have its own \`withBackStack\` call to build the appropriate back stack for that specific \`NavKey\`. \[14:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=891s) You'll get the cleanest code if every matcher you call uses the \`withBackStack\`, which will give you a list of back stack matchers. \[14:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=899s) And when you do find the best match, the match result you get back is a \`BackStackMatchResult\`. \[15:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=904s) This is a sub-class of \`MatchResult\` that adds a new property called \`backStack\`, which is the whole back stack generated by your \`withBackStack\` lambda. \[15:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=914s) This layering approach allowed us to decouple the logic inside the matchers from whatever custom logic you want to use inside your \`withBackStack\` lambda. ### Lightning round, summary, and resources \[15:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=924s) Now, this is a lightning talk, so unfortunately, we're just about out of time, but maybe we can go through a few of the other features that we have in navigation three that you'll find in our nav three recipes. \[15:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=936s) Okay. \[15:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=937s) So, you can add filters to any matcher to short-circuit the matching logic and quickly exclude the matcher based on action, MIME type, or your own custom filters. \[15:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=946s) And this happens before going through any URI parsing or custom serialization, Kotlin Serialization. \[15:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=952s) We also offer a \`StaticKeyDeepLinkMatcher\`, specifically for cases where you don't need to do any parsing to get your \`NavKey\`, but you still want to apply filters. \`\`\`kotlin @Serializable object ImagesKey: NavKey // custom filter val mimeTypeFilter = DeepLinkMatcher.mimeTypeFilter("image/jpg") val matcher = StaticKeyDeepLinkMatcher(ImagesKey, listOf(mimeTypeFilter)) \`\`\` \[16:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=961s) This is perfect for handling action- or MIME-type-only deep links, such as a photo-editing app that can handle opening JPEG images. \[16:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=970s) And speaking of action and MIME type, you can attach any custom \`RequestExtras\` to your \`DeepLinkRequest\`, which your custom filters and \`DeepLinkRequest\` subclasses can use as part of their logic. \[16:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=980s) This lets you mix in AB testing frameworks or external signals. \[16:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=984s) And we also have a whole type-safe APIs for the extras. \`\`\`kotlin val extras = requestExtras { put(SectionExtrasKey, "A") } \`\`\` \[16:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=988s) Oh, and just about all this logic is in Nav3's common KMP code, so all your matchers and back stack logic can be shared across platforms. \[16:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=997s) So, if you want to take a more leisurely look through how Navigation 3 supports deep links, check out our Nav3 recipes. \[16:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=1006s) Yes, and we've also
