entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/declarative-agent-ready-android-builds-with-lightbuild.txt" target="_blank">Declarative, agent-ready Android builds with Lightbuild - Speakers: Scott Myers (Developer Relations Engineer), Juan Sebastian Oviedo (Senior Product Manager) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/declarative-agent-ready-android-builds-with-lightbuild ## About the talk As Android apps grow and AI coding assistants become essential, using executable code to configure your build can create bottlenecks with slow sync times, fragile logic, and added complexity. Enter Lightbuild: Google's declarative, config-driven interface to the build engine, designed for modern Android development. In this session, we'll explore Lightbuild's new approach to managing builds and how to use it to build a demo app. Learn how decoupling build config from execution delivers faster project opens with lightning-fast sync in Android Studio, while offering a predictable schema for safer, more reliable AI editing. We'll also cover Lightbuild's agent-friendly CLI tools for creating reproducible builds across local machines, teams, and CI/CD pipelines ## Summary - Lightbuild is an experimental build system preview for Android apps that replaces executable scripts with purely declarative data files. It uses Gradle as its execution engine under the hood. - Declarative YAML configuration models project structure as a deterministic, static graph. This allows AI agents to inspect topology and safely modify modules or dependencies using a structured schema. - Fast IDE sync bypasses script evaluation by precomputing dependencies into checked-in \`resolved.deps\` files. These files can also serve as lock files during CI/CD builds. - Every project separates code into library modules while keeping application modules as empty shells. This structure accelerates builds and allows distinct application modules to represent flavors such as demo and prod. - A standalone CLI includes commands such as \`query\` and \`resolve\` that can output JSON for agentic workflows. Lightbuild is currently available in Android Studio Canary for experimental use. ## Resources - \[Lightbuild documentation\](https://goo.gle/lightbuild) ## Topics android-builds, lightbuild, android-studio, declarative-build, ai-agents ## Transcript ### Introduction to Lightbuild \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=6s) Hello, everyone. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=7s) My name is Juan Sebastian Oviedo. \[00:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=9s) I am a product manager in the Android Developer Experience team. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=13s) I'm here with Scott, and today we are excited to share with you an early look at Lightbuild, a new experimental build experience for Android apps. \[00:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=22s) I'll go over the context for this project, the philosophy behind it, and why we believe that now is the right time to rethink how Android projects are configured. \[00:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=32s) I'll also go over how this new approach sets us up for the future of Android app development. \[00:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=40s) Let's start with some context on how things work today. \[00:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=44s) Gradle and imperative build scripts give developers the ability to programmatically define almost anything about their builds. \[00:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=51s) You can, for example, have a logic that dynamically computes version codes based on Git history, or define a custom task that transforms assets. \`\`\`kts // build.gradle.kts android { compileSdk = 37 buildTypes { debug { // Custom logic in build script val commit = providers.exec { commandLine("git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD") }.standardOutput.asText.get() .trim() versionNameSuffix = "-$commit" } } } \`\`\` \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=61s) Alongside Gradle, there's AGP or the Android Gradle Plugin, which takes Gradle's general-purpose engine and adapts it to the Android toolchain. \[01:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=72s) Together, Gradle and AGP form a dynamic system that powers the build configuration experience for millions of production apps today. \[01:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=83s) Due to this flexibility, our development tools operate within a specific architectural life cycle. \[01:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=90s) When you open a project, you switch branches or you edit a build file, the IDE needs to have a clear map, a clear understanding of your project configuration, so it can power features like code completion and code navigation. \[01:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=104s) Because build files are written in an imperative, Turing-complete language, the only general way for the IDE to know what the configuration is for it to run the build scripts. \[01:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=116s) During IDE sync, the build system goes through a configuration phase. \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=120s) It evaluates your build scripts, it executes plugin logic, and it constructs the project model. \[02:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=126s) This aligns Android Studio's view of your project with your actual project configuration. \[02:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=134s) As developers, the thing you care about most is delivering a great Android app and getting it to your users. \[02:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=140s) However, managing build scripts, keeping AGP up to date, and keeping the project in sync with the IDE takes time and effort. \[02:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=150s) There are several initiatives across both Google and the broader ecosystem working to improve the developer experience in this area. \[02:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=158s) Initiatives like Declarative Gradle and the Kotlin toolchain aim to replace executable build scripts with declarative build configuration. \[02:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=168s) In Android Studio, we have the AGP Upgrade Assistant, which guides you through the changes needed to go from one version of AGP to another. \[02:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=177s) We also provide an upgrade skill that agents can install and follow to upgrade AGP. \[03:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=184s) Additionally, we are investing in areas like phased sync and resilient sync, so that developers have a better experience when syncing and importing their projects. \[03:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=195s) Each of these efforts targets a piece of the puzzle so that developers can spend more time creating their apps and less time building their projects, managing their build files, and syncing their projects. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=209s) Alongside this efforts, we asked ourselves a broader question. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=214s) What if we reimagined the way projects are configured from the ground up? \[03:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=219s) When we look at the way modern Android apps are architected today, we see a major shift toward heavy modularization. \[03:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=227s) Large code bases often have dozens, or even hundreds of modules: UI modules, feature modules, domain modules, and data modules. \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=237s) And while the root application might occasionally need custom packaging, the vast majority of those library modules follow a standardized repeatable pattern. \[04:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=247s) They don't actually need to have arbitrary executable code in their build files. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=252s) All they need is a clear way to state their structure and their dependencies. ### Core pillars of Lightbuild \[04:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=260s) That observation led us to create Lightbuild. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=261s) Lightbuild rests on two pillars. \[04:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=266s) First, it uses a declarative syntax for configuration, providing for a clear separation between build configuration and logic. \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=274s) And second, it delivers a fast IDE sync experience through ahead-of-time dependency resolution. \[04:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=281s) I'll go over each of these pillars in detail so you can see how they impact your daily workflow. \[04:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=287s) Let's start with the pillar of declarative build configuration. \[04:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=292s) Take a look at the file on the left side of the screen. \[04:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=295s) This represents the configuration for a module today. \`\`\`kts // build.gradle.kts plugins { alias(libs.plugins.android.library) alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose) } val gitCommit = providers.exec { commandLine("git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD") }.standardOutput.asText.get().trim() android { namespace = "com.example.app" compileSdk = 37 defaultConfig { minSdk = 24 buildConfigField("String", "GIT_COMMIT", "\\"$gitCommit\\"") } buildFeatures { compose = true buildConfig = true } } dependencies { implementation(platform(libs.androidx.compose.bom)) implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui) implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.graphics) ... \`\`\` \[04:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=299s) Because this file is executable code, it can have local variable definitions, calls to custom helper functions or convention plugins, conditional statements and in-line task definitions. \[05:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=312s) In order for the IDE to know what this configuration resolves to, it Add credentials in Play Console under Sign-in details, and ensure they bypass two-factor authentication or captchas. - App declarations in Play Console must match the manifests of active bundles across all tracks. Deactivate obsolete version codes so abandoned testing builds do not trigger policy rejections. - App developers are responsible for content produced by third-party generative AI and user data handled by SDKs. Use mechanisms to filter AI output and check the Google Play SDK Index. - Appeals let you communicate with real reviewers after rejections or request extra time to fix policy warnings. Do not resubmit an unchanged app, as repetitive rejections can trigger removals or suspensions. - The advance notice form in Play Console allows developers to submit proof of permission before publishing. Providing authorization documentation upfront protects your submission against impersonation policy rejections. ## Resources - \[Developer Policy Center\](https://goo.gle/play-policy-center) - \[Policy Bytes playlist\](https://goo.gle/policy-bytes-playlist) - \[Play policy insights in Android Studio\](https://d.android.com/studio/publish/insights) - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Topics play-policy, google-play-console, app-review, developer-accounts, android-studio ## Transcript ### Introduction and policy resources overview entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/delivering-seamless-sign-in-and-digital-credentials-on-android.txt" target="_blank">Delivering seamless sign in and digital credentials on Android - Speakers: Chiping Yeh (Developer Relations Engineer), Tom Colvin (CTO, Apptaura) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/delivering-seamless-sign-in-and-digital-credentials-on-android ## About the talk As the industry moves away from passwords and physical wallets, delivering a modern user journey demands both seamless authentication and trusted identity verification. While passkeys establish secure one tap logins, switching devices remains one of the largest drop off points in user engagement. Learn how to reduce migration friction using the Restore Credentials API to meet the new Google Play Zero Tap Sign In standard. This session explores how a single integration with Android Credential Manager unifies passkeys, silent device restoration, and Digital Credentials, allowing you to verify identity attributes directly from the device and build an effortless, secure onboarding flow. ## Summary - Jetpack Credential Manager provides a unified API for passkeys and passwords. It handles the authentication interface and cryptographic operations without developers needing to write UI code. - Conditional Create lets apps upgrade password users to passkeys silently in the background after a successful password autofill. This opportunistically generates and stores a passkey without interrupting the user. - Google Play will require zero-tap sign-in by April 2027 to maintain full publishing capabilities. Apps can meet this requirement by generating a restore key using the Restore Credentials API. - The Digital Credentials API coordinates exchanges between credential holders and verifiers. Holders retain sharing control, while credential payloads stay end-to-end encrypted and inaccessible to Google. - Email and phone number verification replace one-time passwords and magic links with verified digital credentials. Users give consent directly in the Credential Manager bottom sheet without leaving your app. ## Skills - \[Restore Credentials skill\](https://goo.gle/restore-credentials-skill) ## Resources - \[Android passkey demo code\](https://goo.gle/android-passkey-demo) - \[Android identity code samples\](https://goo.gle/android-identity-samples) - \[Zero-tap restoration guide and policy\](https://goo.gle/zero-tap-restoration) - \[Digital Credentials sample app\](https://goo.gle/digital-credentials-sample) ## Topics android, credential-manager, passkeys, restore-credentials, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-immersive-experiences-with-3d-engines-in-jetpack-compose-for-xr.txt" target="_blank">Elevate immersive experiences with 3D Engines in Jetpack Compose for XR - Speakers: Luke Hopkins (Android XR Developer Relations Engineer), Joshua Lorett (Android Staff Engineer), Rodrigo Sanchez (Software Developer - Beyond Sports) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-immersive-experiences-with-3d-engines-in-jetpack-compose-for-xr ## About the talk Learn how to integrate 3D game engines (Godot \& Unity) with Jetpack Compose into a single codebase for mobile and Android XR. We'll explore embedding 3D scenes into spatial containers, setting up Kotlin-to-engine communication ---featuring an exclusive look into how the NBA built their live basketball experience on Android XR. ## Summary - The OpenXR Spatial Containers extension allows 3D engines to share space with native Android UI. Instead of taking over the skybox, real-time engines run inside a managed 3D volume alongside Jetpack XR spatial panels. - Developers can embed real-time engines directly into Jetpack Compose applications as AAR libraries. This approach lets native Android handle business logic and UI while the engine renders 3D components. - Embedding Godot requires an AAR dependency and an AAPT build rule to keep hidden assets. A \`GodotPlugin\` subclass then handles bidirectional communication with Kotlin. - Compose UI loops must stay decoupled from continuous engine tick loops. Blindly forwarding engine updates triggers constant recomposition and causes UI lag. - The NBA app integrates Unity as an embedded library in a separate process using AIDL for inter-process communication, protecting the host app from crashes. ## Resources - \[Android XR developer documentation\](https://developer.android.com/develop/xr) ## Topics android-xr, jetpack-compose, management settings. \[19:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1162s) We used no XR input package, as all the input is handled natively, outside of Unity. \[19:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1169s) Next, in the player settings, you'll want to set your project to use a minimum API level of 24 or above, and the application entry point must be set to the newer Game Activity. \[19:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1178s) Mind that Activity must be left unchecked. Background, so that you can multitask with other apps, and keep the 3D simulation running on the side. \[19:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1195s) We also enable Resizeable Activity, as it is required to render dialogues, such as system permission requests. \[20:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1201s) Lastly, it is recommended for Android XR apps to be rendered using the Universal Render Pipeline and Vulkan Graphics API. \[20:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1208s) In your URP asset, HDR and post-processing should be disabled. \[20:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1215s) Once you have all of those steps done, you're ready to make a build. \[20:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1219s) Move over to the build window, and if you're using Unity 6.1 or above, you can select the Android XR build profile, which lets you separate settings if you also build for Android Mobile. \[20:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1228s) Before building, make sure to enable export project. \[20:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1231s) After Unity finishes building, you will be left with a working Android project which can be assembled in Android Studio and run on a device like any other Unity APK. \[20:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1241s) Once in Android Studio, you'll want to turn your exported build into a library to be used by another application. \`\`\`kts // The Unity build include(":unityLibrary") project(":unityLibrary").projectDir = File("..\\\\Libraries\\\\unityBuild\\\\unityLibrary") // Custom communication IPC module include(":nativeCommunications") project(":nativeCommunications").projectDir = File("..\\\\Libraries\\\\nativeCommunications") // If using XR features include(":unityLibrary:xrmanifest.androidlib") // Used for merging libraries, exporting and publishing. include(":packageExporter") dependencyResolutionManagement { repositories { flatDir { // Required to load unity correctly dirs("${project(":unityLibrary").projectDir}/libs") } } \`\`\` \[20:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1247s) In our project here, we have four different modules: the main APK module to test as a mock-up placeholder for NBA's wrapping application, the Unity Library module holding our exported build, a \`nativeCommunications\` module holding our communication layer that we built between the activities, and a \`packageExporter\` module, which we use to merge our AARs into a single package to deliver to Maven. \[21:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1268s) Merging multiple AARs can be achieved using Android Fused Library, or older community methods like the Fat AAR. \[21:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1275s) You can keep your structure and communication simple by keeping Unity and the main activity running in the same process. \[21:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1282s) We opted against this, and decided to separate the Unity activity into its own process as a safeguard in the event that if the Unity portion would crash, then the NBA app is unaffected and can safely handle closing Unity gracefully without crashing itself. \[21:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1296s) The decision force us to adopt a more robust inter-process communication system. \[21:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1302s) Since the activities are in different processes, there is no memory shared between them, and many common Android IPC methods don't work or fall short of requirements. \[21:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1311s) We use the Android Interface Definition Language, or AIDL, to talk between the NBA's main activity and our embedded Unity activity. \[21:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1318s) Then, communication between Android and Unity is also based in interfaces, making use of the built-in \`AndroidJavaProxy\` in Unity to register a Kotlin interface to a C# interface implementation. \[22:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1331s) Our communications module is primarily focused on what we call the activity bridge. \`\`\`kotlin // Main Activity val intent = Intent(context, AIDLBridgeService::class.java) context.startService(intent) context.bindService(intent, connection, 0) fun onStartMatchClicked() { bridge.runWithService { service -\> service.startMatch("match_id") } } // AIDL Bridge Service private val remoteBinder = object : IBridgeService.Stub() { override fun startMatch(matchID: String?) { addToCallbackQueue { nativeInterface?.startMatch(matchID) } } } \`\`\` \[22:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1335s) Both activities have access to the activity bridge and the utility methods within it. \[22:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1340s) The bridge contains a reference to a service that implements the AIDL interfaces that we defined, and it also provides an easy way for the activities to bind to the process, sorry, to the service and internally manages the lifecycle of it. \[22:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1352s) Starting a simulation can be done with a callback in which we pass the match ID as a parameter. \[22:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1356s) Then, the bridge passes it through AIDL, and then, onto the Unity app, where C# gets a command and starts configuring the scene. \`\`\`csharp public class NativeInterfaceListener : AndroidJavaProxy { \[UsedImplicitly\] public void startMatch(string matchID) { UnityThreadHelper.InvokeOnMain(() =\> _internalAPI.StartMatch(matchID)); } } \`\`\` \[22:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1364s) We do need to wait for Unity to be alive and ready to press the commands that we pass onto it. \[22:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1369s) The Unity activity that wraps the application will be active before Unity itself is. \[22:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1374s) In the case of commands that are sent too early, we store them in a callback queue. \`\`\`kotlin fun onStartMatchClickedInternal() { if (isServiceBound) { AIDLBridgeService.startMatch("match_id") } else { delayedCallbacksQueue.add(action) } } \`\`\` \[22:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1377s) After Unity is done boot loading, and initializing, and we are in a state that we consider safe, we communicate from C# that Unity is ready. \`\`\`csharp // After bootload and initialization using AndroidJavaClass nativeBridge = new("com.company.UnityActivity"); using AndroidJavaObject instance = nativeBridge.GetStatic("instance"); instance.Call("onUnityReady"); \`\`\` \[23:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1386s) After which, we loop over our queue and forward all of our stored commands. \`\`\`kotlin @Suppress("unused") // Unity implicit call fun onUnityReady() { bridge.activityBridgeServiceInternal?.onUnityReady() } delayedCallbacksQueue.forEach { it(activityBridgeService) } \`\`\` \[23:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1392s) This diagram illustrates better how our inter-process communication works. \[23:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1395s) As you can see, using the bridge between activities, we can handle those callbacks that we mentioned. \[23:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1400s) We set up StateFlows that are updated from Unity to monitor values such as authentication status or the current state timestamp of the match. \[23:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1407s) Additionally, we also manage the encryption of credentials, and we forward any errors from Unity so that the NBA can debug easier and decide how to best handle them at an application level. \[23:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1417s) That's it for me. \[23:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1418s) Now, I'll pass the stage back to Josh so he can talk more about how they integrate the Court View Unity package into the NBA app. \[23:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1430s) We use these Gradle dependencies to integrate Unity as a library with our Jetpack Compose app: XR Runtime to access the 3D session, Jetpack \`SceneCore\` to host our Unity activity and toggle spatial environments, and Jetpack Compose for XR to access spatial panels in our Compose code. \`\`\`kts dependencies { implementation("androidx.xr.runtime:runtime:1.0.0") implementation("androidx.xr.scenecore:scenecore:1.0.0") implementation("androidx.xr.compose:compose:1.0.0-beta02") } \`\`\` \[24:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1450s) Next, let's see how we render Court View in Jetpack Compose. \`\`\`kotlin // Step 1: Request Full Space LocalSession.current?.scene?.requestFullSpace() // Step 2: A shared Subspace for NBA app content and embedded Unity Activity. override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?){ setContent { Subspace { SpatialPanel { AppContent() } // Court View val intent = courtViewFeature.intent val controller = rememberSpatialActivityPanelController(intent) SpatialActivityPanel(controller) } } } \`\`\` \[24:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1454s) Before we launch Court View, we bring you into full space. \[24:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1456s) This is required in order to display the spatial panel holding Unity. \[24:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1461s) Next, we send game information over AIDL to launch Court View for a specific game. \[24:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1466s) Unity itself is then started. \[24:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1468s) Our Android archive sends this as an intent to a Unity activity, and we wrap this in a SpatialActivityPanelController. \[24:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1476s) From there, we just pass that controller to a \`SpatialActivityPanel\`. \[24:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1481s) This panel is what holds Court View, and it's shared in our subspace with our main spatial panel. \[24:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1488s) This allows us to both control both of them at once without any issues. \[24:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1495s) And that's it. \[24:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1495s) I'll send it back to Luke. ### Conclusion and resources \[25:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1503s) Thank you very much. \[25:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1504s) As you can see, NBA was able to accelerate Court View by splitting the Unity and Jetpack Compose development. \[25:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1511s) To learn more on getting started with spatial containers and using it within your own Android XR apps, check out developer documentation on developer.android.com/develop/xr. \[25:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1522s) Thank you very much for joining us today, and we can't wait to see what you build.</a>

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-your-apps-with-the-latest-graphics-features-in-jetpack-compose-and-android.txt" target="_blank">Elevate your apps with the latest graphics features in Jetpack Compose and Android - Speakers: Rebecca Franks (Developer Relations Engineer), Aayush Chaudhary (Software Engineer), Rahul Ray (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-your-apps-with-the-latest-graphics-features-in-jetpack-compose-and-android ## About the talk Ready to take your Android UI from "it works" to "it's a work of art"? Join us for a tour of the latest graphics capabilities in Jetpack Compose. We'll show you how to build new visual effects, from delightful mesh gradients to progressive blurs, and using the powerful new graphics features in Android. We will also show you how to improve the performance of your graphics features, without sacrificing battery life or frame rates. ## Summary - Compose 1.12 introduces mesh gradients for rich multicolor blends across a 2D grid of vertices. On Android 14 and above, you can use the native drawMesh API to build custom geometry-driven visual effects. - Compose supports wide color gamuts to provide smoother gradient blending on supported hardware. Enable wide color gamut mode on your activity or window only when displaying rich media. - Compose 1.13 introduces native \`PolygonShape\` and \`MorphPolygonShape\` APIs for custom geometries. \`MorphPolygonShape\` reads progress during the outline resolution phase, updating shapes frame by frame without triggering recomposition. - Compose 1.13 adds progressive blur, while API level 37.2 introduces \`RenderNode.setBackdropRenderEffect\` for sampling background content. Developers can chain backdrop effects together to create frosted-glass or magnifying effects. - Optimize graphics performance by avoiding unnecessary work across frames. Decode only needed image pixels off the main thread and wrap animating effects in a \`graphicsLayer\`. ## Resources - \[Mesh Gradients Documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-mesh) - \[Understanding Color Guide\](https://goo.gle/understanding-color) - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[JetChat Sample App\](https://goo.gle/compose-jetchat) ## Topics jetpack-compose, android-graphics, mesh-gradients, shaders, blurring, color-gamut, performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to graphics features in Jetpack Compose \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=6s) Hi, everyone, and welcome to our session, Elevating Your Apps with the Latest Graphics Features in Compose and Android. \[00:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=12s) My name is Rebecca Franks, and joining me on stage today is-- \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=16s) I am Aayush Chaudhary. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=17s) Hey, I am Rahul Ray. \[00:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=20s) We are seeing an emerging trend in how you are all pushing the boundaries of what's possible on Android and Compose, using AI to really bring your incredible ideas to life. \[00:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=30s) And we love seeing apps that feel premium, native, and delightful. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=36s) We know that apps that feel good and consistently get great ratings from users are ones that generally take advantage of the latest system-level API changes, have continuity between surfaces with shared elements and blurring, they adapt delightfully across form factors, and are performant, and don't leave users guessing, and push the boundaries of what's possible with your device. \[01:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=62s) In this talk today, we're going to show you some of the latest features that help you take advantage of Android, from delighting users with mesh gradients, enabling wide color gamut support, delightful transitions with polygon shapes, what's new in blurring, and, finally, we'll cover how you can think about performance when adding new graphics features into your apps. \[01:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=82s) But throughout the talk today, we'll be covering some of the new APIs at different levels of the stack. \[01:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=87s) While the legacy view UI toolkit is in maintenance mode now, we continue to invest in the underlying Android graphics hardware rendering engines that power Jetpack Compose. \[01:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=99s) You can think of graphics in Android in three different layers: the Compose APIs at the first layer, and this is where all high-level, new UI graphics APIs, like mesh gradient painters, polygon shapes, and progressive blur APIs live. \[01:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=115s) And then we have the intermediate layer, where Compose's DrawScope, draw modifier nodes, and AGSL let you build custom effects. \[02:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=123s) But, finally, we have the Android platform, and Compose can always access a native Canvas and use brand-new OS rendering primitives right inside your Compose modifiers. \[02:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=134s) And we'll show you some of the examples of doing this today. \[02:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=137s) So let's get into it. ### Mesh gradients and custom mesh rendering \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=143s) So first, let's look at mesh gradients, a new API introduced in Compose 1.12. \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=148s) Previously, we have had linear gradients, previously, we have had linear, sweep, and radial gradients, which are great for simple transitions, but if you want rich multicolor blends like ambient backgrounds or floodlighting effects, you need 2D grid of system where, positions and colors can blend across space. \[02:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=167s) Now, to create a mesh gradient like this, first, specify how many rows and columns of patches you want. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { } } \`\`\` \[02:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=175s) And then inside the trailing lambda, call \`setVertex\` and assign a normalized offset ranging from 0F to 1F, along with a color for each grid intersection. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0f, 0.0f), indigo) } } \`\`\` \[03:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=185s) And then to animate those vertices, add animated offsets for eight ver-- vertices. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0f, 0.0f), indigo) // .... setVertex(1, 1, Offset(0.2f, 0.4f) + Offset(animatedOffset, animatedOffset), coral) // .... setVertex(3, 0, Offset(0.0f, 1.0f), sunshine) // .... } } Box( modifier = modifier.padding(32.dp) .safeContentPadding() .aspectRatio(16 / 9f) .fillMaxWidth() .paint(gradientPainter) ) \`\`\` \[03:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=192s) Once your painter is defined, simply call it with any composable via a paint modifier. \[03:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=199s) Now, in the JetChat app, we added a feature to like a message when you double-tap on it. \[03:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=204s) To build this, we set up a 2 by 3 mesh and place our color stops across the component. \`\`\`kotlin MeshGradientPainter( rows = 2, columns = 3, hasBicubicColor = true, ) { // Row 0 (top edge, y = 0.0f) setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0000f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFFF6B6B)) setVertex(0, 1, Offset(0.3300f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFFFD6D6)) setVertex(0, 2, Offset(0.6700f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFE8C3FF)) setVertex(0, 3, Offset(1.0000f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFE396FF)) // ... remaining vertices for Rows 0, 1, and 2 } \`\`\` \[03:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=211s) Notice that we set \`hasBicubicColor\` to true over here. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=214s) By default, colors interpolate linearly across triangles, which can sometimes leave visible patches. \[03:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=220s) Turning this on switches the shader to smooth bicubic interpolation so that colors can melt seamlessly into one another. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=228s) Now, what if you want to build an animated ambient glow like this behind the input box? \[03:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=235s) To approach an effect like this with mesh gradient, you need two things. \[03:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=239s) First, a smooth organic motion for the interior vertices and a way to soften the outer edges so that you don't end up getting a hard rectangle around the card. \[04:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=249s) So we start by setting up a \`rememberInfiniteTransition\` with two phase angles running slightly at different durations so that the motion feels organic rather than mechanical. \`\`\`kotlin val transition = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "userInputGlowMesh") val phase1 by transition.animateFloat( initialValue = 0f, targetValue = (2 \* PI).toFloat(), animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable( animation = tween(durationMillis = 2800, easing = LinearEasing), repeatMode = RepeatMode.Restart, ), label = "glowPhase1", ) val phase2 by transition.animateFloat( initialValue = 0f, targetValue = (2 \* PI).toFloat(), animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable( animation = tween(durationMillis = 4200, easing = LinearEasing), repeatMode = RepeatMode.Restart, ), label = "glowPhase2", ) \`\`\` \[04:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=260s) Here, we animate the interior vertices and we pin the outer rings, outer ring of the vertices with edges with 0 alpha. \[04:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=268s) Because the outer boundary is stationary and transparent, the glow naturally feathers out. \[04:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=273s) And, finally, we feed those animated offsets to our \`MeshGradientPainter\`. \`\`\`kotlin MeshGradientPainter( rows = 6, columns = 5, hasBicubicColor = true, ) { for (r in 0..6) { for (c in 0..5) { val offset = if (r in 1..5 \&\& c in 1..4) { val ampX = when (r) { 1, 2 -\> 0.048f 3 -\> 0.042f 4 -\> 0.028f else -\> 0.036f } val ampY = when (r) { 1, 2 -\> 0.028f 3 -\> 0.020f 4 -\> 0.022f else -\> 0.016f } val d = orbit(c, r, ampX, ampY) Offset( x = (baseU + d.x).coerceIn(0.04f, 0.96f), y = (baseV + d.y).coerceIn(0.05f, 0.95f), ) } else { Offset(baseU, baseV) } setVertex(r, c, offset, gridColors\[r\]\[c\]) } } } \`\`\` \[04:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=282s) The mesh gradient you just saw is drawn using \`drawMesh\` API on Android 14 and above. \[04:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=287s) So let's take a closer look at this API by building an effect from scratch. \[04:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=292s) For JetChat welcome screen, we want to draw a path that looks like a ribbon. \[04:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=296s) Notice two things here: the stroke width is not constant and the color runs along each stroke of the path. \[05:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=303s) Let's break this down and understand what we actually need to build this effect. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevating-camera-experiences-across-devices-with-camerax-and-on-device-intelligence.txt" target="_blank">Elevating camera experiences across devices with CameraX and on-device intelligence - Speakers: Aman Choudhary (Developer Relations Engineer), Scott Nien (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevating-camera-experiences-across-devices-with-camerax-and-on-device-intelligence ## About the talk Users expect third-party apps to capture photos and videos with the same high fidelity as their device's native camera, regardless of lighting conditions or hardware tier. Delivering this consistency across the expanding Android ecosystem comes with key architectural considerations. This session demonstrates how to construct robust, professional capture pipelines that maximize device capabilities while remaining reliable across all form factors. We will explore the latest advancements in CameraX, showing you how to integrate cutting-edge capabilities like Motion Photos and on-device AI enhancements through Google Play services, alongside spatial experiences using the Jetpack XR SDK. We will also look at our CameraX skill, which allows the coding agent of your choice to automatically implement the concepts in this talk, and more! ## Summary - Jetpack CameraX is the recommended camera library for Android apps as Camera1 is deprecated. Play policy enforcements will begin disabling Camera1 next year in Android 18. - \`CameraXViewfinder\` adapts camera previews across different form factors such as foldables. In CameraX 1.7, it adds gesture controls and Screen Flash support. - Audio \& Display Glasses run apps on a host phone while exposing cameras on both devices. Passing \`ProjectedDeviceContext\` allows CameraX to capture images directly from the glasses. - The Feature Group API helps apps select supported combinations of camera capabilities. Starting with CameraX 1.6, it supports combining 4K recording with Video Stabilization. - On-device machine learning analyzes camera previews and captured media through ML Kit and MediaPipe. Developers can run tasks ranging from real-time gesture detection to generative image descriptions. ## Resources - \[Camera talk resources and migration guide\](https://goo.gle/ads-26-camera-talk-res) ## Topics camerax, android-camera, on-device-ml, gemini-nano, mediapipe, ml-kit, android-xr ## Transcript ### Introduction and CameraX overview \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=5s) Hello, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=6s) Welcome to our session. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/enabling-seamless-cross-device-interactions.txt" target="_blank">Enabling seamless cross-device interactions - Speakers: Yacine Rezgui (Developer Relations Engineer), Hanrui Gao (Developer Relations Engineer), Nataraj K R (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/enabling-seamless-cross-device-interactions ## About the talk As users move between phones, wearables, and audio peripherals, delivering fluid cross-device experiences has become essential for engagement. However, relying on standard networking approaches often leads to battery drain, latency spikes, and fragmented user sessions. This deep dive introduces specialized Android APIs built for multi-device communication, offering memory- and power-efficient patterns to keep transitions between devices instant, reliable, and intuitive. ## Summary - Companion Device Manager replaces foreground services for Bluetooth peripherals by waking apps based on presence and managing connections without draining battery. Android 17 adds new profiles specifically for medical devices and fitness trackers. - Jetpack Telecom acts as a system call coordinator for VoIP apps across connected devices like watches and cars, working back to Android 8. It also synchronizes mute and hangup actions via CallControlScope. - Upcoming Jetpack Telecom 1.1.0 features include unified call histories in the system dialer (SDK 36.1+) and automatic 5G network slicing on supported carrier networks. - Quick Share SDK is launching next year so developers can embed local, end-to-end encrypted file sharing directly into Android and iOS apps. Tap to share (launched with Pixel 11) can even automatically wake a closed receiving app. ## Resources - \[Devices per person in 2023 chart\](https://www.statista.com/chart/32691/average-number-of-devices-and-connections-per-capita/) ## Topics cross-device, companion-device-manager, jetpack-telecom, quick-share, bluetooth, voip, peer-to-peer ## Transcript ### Introduction to cross-device interactions \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=5s) Hi, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=6s) Welcome to Enabling Seamless Cross-Device Interactions. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=11s) I'm Hanrui, and today I'm joined by my colleagues, Yacine and Nataraj. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=17s) When we talk about connectivity, what often comes to mind is a basic network link or Bluetooth headsets. \[00:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=24s) On Android, connectivity is much broader than that. \[00:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=28s) It's really about making devices work better together. \[00:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=33s) Today, we will walk through common cross-device scenarios and show you which API is right for each one. \[00:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=41s) For quite a long time, we used to build apps for a single device, phone only. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=48s) Then wearables took off. \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=50s) Soon it became very common to have a smartwatch paired with a phone, syncing data in the background or taking calls directly. \[01:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=60s) Add ear-- add wireless earbuds. \[01:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=63s) Now, users switch audio device mid-call, from watch to phone to earbuds or over to their cars. We will explore the technical benefits of the unified Jetpack Glance API and the new Remote Compose engine, detailing how they seamlessly align with Modern Android Development. Finally, we will share the latest UX guidance and walk through practical migration strategies to help you build the next generation of glanceable UI. ## Summary - Wear OS is evolving full-screen Tiles into Wear Widgets built with Jetpack Glance and powered by Remote Compose. - Remote Compose shares the same compiler and runtime as Jetpack Compose UI while safely decoupling your UI from the app process. - Small and large container sizes align with mobile grid formats, while Jetpack Glance Wear APIs maintain backward compatibility down to Wear 4. - Migrating existing Tiles to widgets can use either a recommended dual-service strategy or a single compatibility service. ## Skills - \[Tiles to widgets migration skill\](https://goo.gle/skills-repo) ## Resources - \[Tile to widget service migration\](https://goo.gle/wearos-tiles-widgets-migration) - \[Horologist media sample app\](https://goo.gle/media-sample) - \[Wear Widgets getting started guide\](https://goo.gle/wear-widgets) ## \[06:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=395s) We're going to build our own app component on top of Material 3 switch button. \[06:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=400s) On the left, we have the standard Wear Compose component you'd write inside your app, and on the right is the Remote Compose version. \`\`\`kotlin // Wear Compose @Composable fun HistoryEraserButton( onClick: () -\> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier, checked: Boolean = true, onCheckedChange: (Boolean) -\> Unit = {}, ) \`\`\` \`\`\`kotlin // Wear RemoteCompose @RemoteComposable @Composable fun RemoteHistoryEraserButton( onClick: Action, modifier: RemoteModifier = RemoteModifier, checked: RemoteBoolean = true.rb, onCheckedChange: Action = Action.Empty, ) \`\`\` \[06:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=412s) Notice how similar the patterns are. \[06:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=415s) When writing Remote Compose code, however, you'll use the \`RemoteComposable\` annotation. defining the execute to the code to execute inside the lambda, you'll need to declare an action such as launching a pending intent, calling a service, or updating a value. RemoteSplitSwitchButtonDefaults.splitSwitchButtonColors( checkedContainerColor = colors.errorContainer, ... ), label = { RemoteText("History Eraser".rs) }, secondaryLabel = { RemoteText("Don't touch it!".rs) }, ) \`\`\` \[07:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=473s) And finally, let's see the result. padding, corner radius, we build on the standard preview annotation, but with an additional parameter provider to inject these configurations. \`\`\`kotlin @Preview(name = "Squircle Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetSquirclePreview( @PreviewParameter(SquircleAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) @Preview(name = "Round Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetRoundPreview( @PreviewParameter(RoundAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) \`\`\` \[08:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=518s) The library provides preconfigured \`PreviewParameter\` provider implementations that match real-world Wear OS devices. \[08:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=530s) These preview annotations let you easily verify your layout across very various different hardware shapes. \[08:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=538s) Beyond testing your layouts, you can use these previews to generate the static images required for the on-device widget picker. \`\`\`kotlin @Preview(name = "Widget Picker Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetRectangularPreview( @PreviewParameter(RectangularAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) \`\`\` \[09:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=545s) The library provides a parameter for rectangular preview shape which emulates the full uncropped rectangular containers. ### Sample implementation and migration tools \[09:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=557s) And if you want to see how exactly this works in practice, we've refreshed our Horologist media sample app to include a new widget that showcases this API. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=567s) We show how to add both the small and large versions of the media widget. \[09:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=575s) Check it out on GitHub to see side-by-side the comparison of the legacy ProtoLayout code and the new Remote Compose implementation. \[09:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=583s) We're sure you'll like it. \[09:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=587s) Finally, this wouldn't be a, you know, a talk without mentioning AI. \[09:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=592s) To speed up your migration, we've published a new tiles to widgets migration skill on GitHub. \[09:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=598s) You can use it with your agent of choice, or you can add it directly to Android Studio using the Android CLI. \`\`\`shell android skills add wear-widgets android skills add --all \`\`\` \[10:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=604s) Now I'll hand you back to François to wrap things up. ### Summary and wrap-up \[10:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=612s) Thank you. \[10:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=612s) Thank you, Yuri. \[10:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=613s) So as you can see, evolving your tiles into Wear Widgets is a very straightforward process. \[10:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=619s) To recap, by migrating to Jetpack Glance Wear and Remote Compose, you are not simply updating your UI, you are joining a more unified Android widgets ecosystem. \[10:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=631s) You can now build beautiful, backward compatible widgets using a modern, declarative framework fully aligned with Jetpack Compose. \[10:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=640s) You can start migrating your tiles today by heading over to the Getting Started guide on Android Developers site for more-- for all the details. \[10:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=650s) We look forward to seeing all the expressive, glanceable experiences you build for the wrist. \[10:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=655s) Thank you very much for joining us today, this morning, and we hope you enjoy the rest of the conference. This session provides a practical guide to getting started. Using code examples and learning from real-life case studies, we'll walk through the development lifecycle: building, testing, and publishing your first connected app to reach users within their AI-powered workflows. By the end of this session, you'll be able to: - Integrate your service with the Connected Apps Platform. - Test your integration across different AI surfaces. - Publish your app's features into users' AI workflows. ## Summary - The Connected Apps Platform provides a single entry point to launch app capabilities across Gemini and Search using declarative schemas. It will open in phases, starting with a preview for US developers. - Integrations use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard through either remote servers or local on-device servers via the AppFunctions Jetpack library. Remote servers can also return custom UI rendered inside an iframe. - Confirmations scale with risk to protect user trust. Developers mark tools as read-only or with \`destructiveHint\`, helping Gemini ask for explicit confirmation when actions modify or delete data. - Gemini Developer Mode lets you inspect tool calls and latency against public endpoints. It is available now to developers in the US. - Google Connected Console handles the production rollout for approved developers. You configure endpoints, manage testers across selected surfaces, and submit your app for review. ## Resources - \[Connected Apps preview sign-up\](https://developers.google.com/connected-apps) - entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-gemini-nano-and-gemma-4-powering-on-device-intelligence.txt" target="_blank">Inside Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 powering on-device intelligence - Speakers: Sara Smoot (Engineering Lead Gemma) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ekS4_gV6Ojc - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-gemini-nano-and-gemma-4-powering-on-device-intelligence ## About the talk Gemma 4 brings capable, multimodal AI directly to Android devices. In this session, we'll trace how Gemma evolved into a model family built for efficiency and explore what the edge-optimized E2B and E4B models can do on-device, from vision and audio understanding to agentic function calling. We'll cover the architecture behind that efficiency, including Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), and show how Gemma and Gemini Nano work together through AICore. You'll learn how Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) preserves model capability within 1.1--3.5 GB RAM footprints, while Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) accelerates decoding speeds 1.5x--3x for responsive, real-time experiences. ## Summary - Gemma 4 models expand on-device multimodal capabilities with 128K-token context on E2B/E4B under an Apache 2 license. - Multi-token prediction drafter models cut decode latency by 40% and save 30% to 40% energy. They share the base model's KV cache to avoid regenerating prefills. - Quantization-aware training compresses the custom mobile quantization checkpoint to under 1 GB using targeted 2-bit quantization. - Android applications can integrate the models hands-off through AICore as Gemini Nano 4, or bundle them with LiteRT for custom fine-tunes. ## Resources - \[Gemma 4 model card\](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/model_card_4) - \[Gemini Nano on Android\](https://developer.android.com/ai/gemini-nano) - \[Gemma 4 on Hugging Face\](https://huggingface.co/collections/google/gemma-4) - \[Gemma 4 on Kaggle\](https://kaggle.com/models/google/gemma-4) ## Topics gemini-nano, gemma-4, on-device-ai, mobile-ml, aicore, litert, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-the-first-wave-on-googlebook-with-notability-and-logitech.txt" target="_blank">Inside the first wave on Googlebook with Notability and Logitech - Speakers: Emilie Roberts (Developer Relations Engineer), Ryan Shea (Head of Android), Joe Yezhou Wang (Engineering manager at Logitech) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aZjbDY3UXws - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-the-first-wave-on-googlebook-with-notability-and-logitech ## About the talk The launch of Googlebook opens up a new frontier for high-fidelity, desktop-grade experiences. In this session, we go behind the scenes with two pioneering partners who built for this platform from the ground up. Notability will share their journey creating a desktop-class Android app using Jetpack Compose. Learn about their journey moving from other app platforms with desktop top-of-mind. Second, Logitech will dive into the hardware side, discussing how they are building and customizing peripherals to integrate seamlessly with Googlebook. Join the session to get practical, real-world insights on optimizing inputs, leveraging large-screen APIs, and delivering a premium, cohesive user experience across hardware and software. ## Summary - Jetpack Compose and Navigation 3 make it easy to adapt layouts across devices based on available window size rather than device form factors. - Desktop-class experiences require supporting multi-input models such as keyboards and trackpads. Features like Continue On in Android 17 also let users hand off tasks between devices. - Jetpack Ink gives developers a low-latency drawing pipeline without having to manage custom rendering threads or complex layer handoffs. - The allowlisted Peripheral Customization API lets developers map peripheral hardware triggers to OS actions using vendor and product IDs. ## Topics googlebook, jetpack-compose, jetpack-ink, navigation-3, large-screens, peripheral-customization, kotlin-multiplatform ## Transcript ### Introduction to building for Googlebook entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/insights-into-agent-code-generation-from-android-bench.txt" target="_blank">Insights into agent code generation from Android Bench - Speakers: Tomáš Mlynarič (Android DevRel) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/insights-into-agent-code-generation-from-android-bench ## About the talk AI models can generate entire features in minutes, but is the code correct? We built Android Bench, our AI evaluation benchmark, to answer this question after analyzing thousands of generated code changes. This talk shares insights from our journey, including all the ways we saw models cheats, how prompt specificity leads to higher code quality and how different agents approach the same task. ## Summary - Android Bench 2.0 uses closed-source tasks to prevent contamination and evaluate AI coding agents on complex Android development work. - Evaluation relies on implementation-agnostic UI tests and a Multimodal LLM Judge instead of brittle unit tests or strict pixel-diffing. - Built-in cheating detectors catch agent shortcuts such as test tampering or fake background drawables. Any detected shortcut results in an immediate failing grade. - Cost per task varies widely from advertised token prices because talkative models burn more tokens by repeatedly rebuilding and rerunning. - Frontier models achieve around 80% completion rates but pass only 20% to 40% of tasks due to subtle flaws. ## Resources - \[Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities\](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified) - \[Android Bench leaderboard and benchmarks\](https://d.android.com/bench) ## Topics android-bench, benchmarking, llm-evaluation, code-generation, ai-agents ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android Bench \*\*Tomáš Mlynarič\*\* \[00:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=4s) Morning, everyone. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/integrate-your-app-with-the-android-intelligence-system.txt" target="_blank">Integrate your app with the Android intelligence system - Speakers: Sarah Shamsie (Product Manager at Google), Dan Galpin (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UsqDEfyOH2E - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/integrate-your-app-with-the-android-intelligence-system ## About the talk Android is evolving into an intelligence system where agents like Gemini orchestrate tasks across apps. To unlock new user experiences and participate in these agentic workflows, your app must expose its core capabilities. This session is a practical guide to integrating your app with Android's intelligence layer. We'll survey key integration paths - including on-device Android MCP, server-side MCP, and Task Automation - and provide a decision framework for choosing the right path for your use case. We'll also explore proactive experiences with Personal Context. You will learn how to: - Select the optimal integration path for your app's needs. - Implement both reactive and proactive intelligence features. - Balance performance and security in agentic integrations. ## Summary - Android MCP is a unified on-device tool calling framework powered by the Jetpack AppFunctions library. It maps MCP primitives to Kotlin constructs and runs on Android Binder IPC. - On-device tools excel when accessing encrypted data or device sensors. Alternatively, platform-driven Task Automation lets pre-loaded agents simulate touch events without code changes. - Your app acts as an Android MCP server while agents discover and call tools. Declare tools with \`AppFunctionDeclaration\`, provide KDoc descriptions, and avoid relying on Kotlin default values. - The Connected Apps Platform, currently in preview, lets you test your AppFunctions with Gemini. Set up your connected app in Google Connected Console, then upload your bundle in Play Console. ## Resources - \[Jetpacker travel sample app\](https://goo.gle/jetpacker) - \[Sample agent source code\](https://github.com/android/appfunctions) - \[Connected Apps documentation and preview signup\](https://developers.google.com/connected-apps) - \[Android AppFunctions documentation\](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) ## Topics android-mcp, appfunctions, gemini, connected-apps, model-context-protocol, on-device-ai ## Transcript ### Introduction to the entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/lessons-from-whatsapps-wear-os-journey.txt" target="_blank">Lessons from WhatsApp's Wear OS journey - Speakers: Martin Pelant (Software Engineer, Meta), Subhag Bhatia (Software Engineer, Meta) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/lessons-from-whatsapps-wear-os-journey ## About the talk Hear directly from WhatsApp engineers on how they upgraded their Wear OS app at scale. This session covers the architectural and UX decisions behind integrating Material 3 and adopting Wear Widgets. Gain direct insight into the lessons, patterns and tools the team used to update their app and deliver a cohesive user experience. ## Summary - Sharing Android phone code with Wear OS cuts duplicate work but requires dependency injection and manifest overrides. Tests should compare multibinding sets so modularized features do not silently disappear. - Runtime notification bridging management prevents duplicate alerts while letting the watch operate independently. Turning bridging off at login and back on at logout stops phone mirrors from double-buzzing. - Material 3 migrations on round displays require managing behavioral changes alongside visual styling. Using \`TransformingLazyColumn\` properly means applying transformations at only one level and avoiding caching positions with Compose's \`remember\`. - App expiry limits can trigger sudden active user drops if watches fail to update promptly. Scheduled update reminders direct users to Google Play before their ninety-day build expires. ## Topics wear-os, material-3, jetpack-compose, modularization, notifications, tiles-and-widgets ## \[09:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=540s) New messages arrive, rows move, and bubbles come in every shape. \[09:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=546s) Let's see what it meant to get it right. \[09:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=550s) If you notice on the left, bubbles are shrinking way too aggressively. \[09:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=555s) Well, each message is internally a bubble wrapped inside a card. \[09:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=559s) We told the parent card to apply a transform, but the same transform was being passed on to the child bubble as well. \[09:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=566s) As a result, the child bubble is getting twice the amount of intended transform. \[09:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=572s) The fix was to ensure that we apply a transform at one level, and that was at the parent card. \[09:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=577s) And that's also a key principle. \[09:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=579s) We ensured trans- one transform for one item. \[09:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=586s) And here's another problem: bubbles that are small and faded right in the middle of the screen where they should be full-sized. \[09:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=593s) Well, size is a function of their position on the screen. \[09:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=597s) In our initial version, we saved the size fitting using the Compose's remember function, but that also ended up saving its older position. \[10:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=606s) Now as a result, when a new message arrives and it shifts the older bubbles upwards, their transform is still based on their older position. \[10:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=614s) And that results in that bug. \[10:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=617s) To fix this, we stopped saving the size using the remember call and got rid of the call. \[10:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=622s) And that's also a learning. \[10:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=624s) When a row moves, its transformation must move with it. \[10:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=630s) Here you can see both the fixes in the code. \`\`\`kotlin // FIX #1: ONE OWNER CompositionLocalProvider( LocalSurfaceTransformation provides null ) { M3Card(transformation = t) { SharedChatEntry(...) } } // FIX #2: CURRENT ITEM SCOPE val t = SurfaceTransformation(spec) \`\`\` \`\`\`kotlin // BUG #1: DOUBLE MORPH M3Card(transformation = t) { CompositionLocalProvider( LocalSurfaceTransformation provides t ) { SharedChatEntry(...) } } // BUG #2: STALE ITEM SCOPE val t = remember(spec) { SurfaceTransformation(spec) } \`\`\` \[10:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=632s) On the top left, you can see the transform is being applied at two levels, and on the top right, only it's being applied at one level, which is the M3 card. \[10:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=642s) On the bottom left, we are using the remember call to cache the transform, but it also caches the position. \[10:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=649s) And on the bottom right, we are computing the transform considering the bubble's latest position every time. \[10:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=657s) As you can see, the result is a consistent experience across all the screens, where key content stays near the center, and rows move naturally near the edge. ### Handling wrist notification alerts \[11:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=669s) Next, let's talk about notifications. \[11:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=672s) Now imagine your wrist buzzes, you check your watch, and you see a message. \[11:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=676s) But moments later, your wrist buzzes again, and again. \[11:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=681s) You get multiple notifications, and when you check each time, it's the same thing that you see. \[11:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=688s) Well, that's really annoying. \[11:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=689s) So to fix this, we asked ourselves two questions. \[11:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=693s) What event should alert the notification should alert the user? \[11:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=697s) And which event should update the notifications silently? \[11:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=701s) This bug was happening because behind the scene, profile photo updates, media downloads, and receipts, which should silently update the notification, were alerting the user instead. \[11:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=712s) Now, when a new message arrives, the wrist buzzes exactly once, while non-alertworthy events refresh the notification silently. \[12:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=722s) And that's also a lesson. \[12:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=723s) When notification is one of your core user journeys, we must ensure that each alert truly deserves the user's attention. \[12:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=732s) On the topic of notifications. \[12:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=734s) Earlier, WhatsApp Wear OS notifications allowed you to do two things. \[12:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=738s) You could read the message, or you could open the app. \[12:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=742s) If you wanted to reply to a notification directly, you couldn't do that earlier. \[12:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=746s) So we bridged that gap using Android's notification action with RemoteInput API. \[12:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=753s) The user can now type it, say it, or tap a quick reply. \[12:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=757s) But remember, hitting send isn't the end. \[12:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=760s) If a message is sent successfully, we mark the chat as read and clear the notification. \[12:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=766s) If a message fails to deliver, we offer a single-tap retry. \[12:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=770s) And that's also a key learning while developing this, is that a notification action must be treated as a complete end-to-end workflow. ### Migrating from tiles to widgets \[13:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=780s) Next, Tiles and Widgets. \[13:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=782s) A Tile, as you can see, is one full screen, where you can reach by swiping from your watch face. \[13:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=789s) Widgets on the other hand, are multiple smaller cards, where several can fit in one scrollable screen. \[13:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=795s) Both WhatsApp Tiles and Widgets are powered by the same underlying data. \[13:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=801s) And that's also a twist. \[13:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=802s) You might think that this UI is being drawn by our app, but that's actually not the case. \[13:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=807s) We only describe the UI and the data, and the system draws it. \[13:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=814s) And also, tapping on any of the icon can't run your app's code. \[13:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=818s) You can only ask it to open a screen. \[13:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=821s) And that's our lesson. \[13:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=822s) If the system is drawing your UI, it's part of your product and testing metrics. \[13:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=827s) Frank and Yuri will go deeper in their talk on Widgets. ### Preventing the active user cliff with update reminders \[13:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=832s) And that brings me to the last slide, which is let's take a step back and ask ourselves, at the end of the day, we want more and more users using our apps. \[14:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=844s) Now imagine as a developer, you log in to your dashboards one day, and you see a significant active user cliff. \[14:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=851s) Well, at first first of all, it would be very concerning. \[14:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=854s) And then you might start debugging it. \[14:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=856s) And you might feel that there was a crash, or there's some bad release going on. \[14:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=861s) But for us, none of those were the case. \[14:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=862s) It turns out that every WhatsApp app version has a 90-day built-in expiry. \[14:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=869s) So imagine users are stuck on a stale build, while the newer builds are taking time to reach their watches. \[14:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=876s) So as a result, the users are not leaving the app, but still their app stopped working. \[14:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=882s) So we made updating the app part of the product. \[14:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=886s) As you can see on the screen, 15 days before the app expiry, this appears on the screen. \[14:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=891s) Then it appears again at 7, 5, 3, 2, and 1 day remaining. \[14:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=898s) User can choose to dismiss it, or land in the Play Store to update their app. \[15:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=903s) This helps by giving user multiple reminders that their app expiry is approaching, and also giving them multiple chances to update their app. \[15:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=911s) And that's our final learning. \[15:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=913s) Our jobs as developers isn't complete when we ship an update to 100%. \[15:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=917s) It's only complete when users actually receive our updates. \[15:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=923s) That brings us to the end. \[15:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=924s) If you'd like to continue the conversation, please feel free to come say hello during the office hours. \[15:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=930s) And next up is going to be Frank and Yuri to talk about Wear Widgets. \[15:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=933s) Thank you.</a>
