entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/let-agents-generate-ui-in-your-android-apps-with-a2ui.txt" target="_blank">Let agents generate UI in your Android apps with A2UI - Speakers: Anton Beloglazov (Software Engineer), Nick Butcher (Product Manager) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/let-agents-generate-ui-in-your-android-apps-with-a2ui ## About the talk A2UI is transitioning from web-centric components to native Android. The new Jetpack Compose renderer for A2UI v0.9 enables developers to render dynamic, LLM-generated UI natively. Instead of webviews, it leverages a Coroutine-driven actor framework, sealed-class lifecycles, and native Material 3 integration. This session walks through the new architecture, explaining how server-driven component trees translate into reactive Compose nodes, and how built-in layout transitions handle structural updates smoothly without blocking the UI. ## Summary - A2UI provides a declarative, open JSON protocol for agentic back ends to describe dynamic user interfaces instead of text responses. - The protocol revolves around catalogs that define allowed components and functions, along with surfaces that represent agent-controlled UI pieces. - Jetpack Compose's A2UI library renders streamed surface models natively using Material 3 components with built-in accessibility and progressive rendering. - In-memory data models update bound UI elements instantly without contacting the agent, while outbound events route user actions back. - Developers can customize existing catalog items or create custom components to strictly control what the agent can display. ## Resources - \[A2UI Compose documentation\](https://goo.gle/a2ui-compose-docs) - \[Material 3 A2UI demo\](https://goo.gle/material3-a2ui-demo) - \[JetPacker sample app\](https://github.com/android/ai-samples) - \[A2UI specification\](https://a2ui.org) ## Topics a2ui, generative-ui, jetpack-compose, android, ai-agents, material-design ## Transcript ### Introduction to generative UI and A2UI \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=6s) Hi, everyone, and welcome to this talk where we're going to be talking about how to generate UI in your Android apps using our brand new A2UI library. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=14s) My name is Nick Butcher, I'm a product manager working on Jetpack Compose. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=17s) Hey everyone, I'm Anton, I'm an engineer on the Compose team. \[00:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=21s) I'm working on this new Jetpack Compose A2UI renderer that we're very excited to tell you about today. \[00:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=27s) Yes, now with the rise of AI capabilities, many apps are looking at how AI can help you to improve or build new experiences for their users. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=36s) One of the exciting experiences that some people are looking at is generative UI, which is how, at runtime, agentic back ends can create brand new UIs for your users, which we think is very interesting. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=48s) But unfortunately right now, many agentic back ends' responses are trapped in walls of text, like this. \[00:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=55s) So, here's an example where I've asked an a- agent to generate me a new feature for booking a trip. \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=61s) So, here's the prompt. \[01:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=62s) And as you can see, it's given actually quite a decent answer, but it's trapped in this wall of text which I can't really easily interact with and it looks nothing like the rest of my application. \[01:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=73s) Generative UI allows you to create an experience like this instead, where you can generate a new UI on the fly in response to dynamic input, opening up possibilities for more customization, or more new experiences. \[01:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=86s) So, here's an example of a UI that's created using like standard, native components. \[01:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=92s) So, you can absolutely build this kind of experience today yourself, but you'd have to define your own like format for interchange with the back end, your own kind of event stream, and functions, and so on. \[01:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=102s) A2UI, which stands for Agent-to-UI, is an open protocol which is a JSON format for defining all of these things. \[01:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=113s) So, one of the things I really like about A2UI is it's a declarative format. \[01:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=117s) The agent is just returning a JSON representation of the UI to render. \[02:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=121s) It's not returning any code that your client then needs to execute, which can open you up to certain security vulnerabilities. \[02:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=128s) It's just declarative. \[02:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=130s) So, what other concepts do we need to know about A2UI? ### Core concepts: Catalogs and surfaces \[02:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=133s) Just two main concepts: catalogs and surfaces. \[02:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=136s) Catalog has components like text, button, row, and column that the agent can use to build the UI. \[02:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=141s) A catalog also has functions that the agent can use for formatting text, validating user input, or opening URLs. \[02:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=149s) A catalog is a contract that defines what components and functions your app supports, and the agent can only build with those. \[02:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=156s) This means, as Nick mentioned, the agent never executes arbitrary code in your app. \[02:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=160s) It composes a UI from the building blocks that you design and trust. \[02:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=164s) One more important concept is a surface. \[02:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=166s) A surface is one piece of UI that the agent controls, like this trip planner example on the slide. \[02:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=172s) The agent describes the UI for a surface in JSON using the A2UI protocol messages, like \`createSurface\`, \`updateComponents\`, and using the components and functions defined in your catalog. \[03:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=184s) So speaking of catalog, catalog is a very fundamental concept in A2UI, cuz it controls what components that the agent can use to construct an interface. \[03:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=193s) The A2UI spec defines something called the basic catalog, which is a set of common components you can use for constructing most UIs. \[03:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=201s) The Jetpack Compose A2UI renderer provides an implementation of the basic catalog using Material 3 components. \[03:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=207s) Most of the catalog components are ready to use out of the box. \[03:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=210s) There are three media components: image, video, and audio player, where you need to plug in your library of choice. \[03:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=216s) For example, you may choose Coil for image loading and Media3 for the video and audio player. \[03:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=222s) But the real power of A2UI and our new renderer library is that you can create your own, completely custom components and catalogs, and fully control what the agent can use to build the UI. \[03:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=232s) We'll come back to catalogs later. \[03:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=234s) Okay, so let's take a look at what this looks like. \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=237s) So, if we can switch to the demo machine, please. \[04:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=240s) This is our demo app, which we're going to use, and we're going to build up the A2UI renderer to show you how easy it is. \[04:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=245s) So it's a set of prompts, as you can see in these little chips in the middle of the screen, that you can send to an agent. \[04:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=251s) So, if we click on one of the prompts, it's sending that prompt to a real, live agent back end, so fingers crossed for the demo, and in addition to the prompt, we also append some system instructions. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=261s) So, we tell the back end about the A2UI protocol, about the catalog of components, in this case, the basic catalog we're using right here, that it can use to build the UI, and we give it some examples of how to build this. \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=274s) The chat session implementation in our demo app already knows how to extract raw JSON A2UI messages from the agent's responses. \[04:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=282s) So, in this case, the agent replied with some text followed by A2UI protocol messages: \`createSurface\`, \`updateComponents\`. \[04:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=288s) But at the moment, our app just shows this raw JSON and doesn't render it as UI yet. \[04:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=294s) Okay, before we dive in and implement the code, if we can switch back to the slides just for 1 second, let's take a step back and tell you about the system design, which we're going to use to implement this. \[05:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=304s) Oh, here we go. ### Application architecture and message processing \[05:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=307s) Yeah, so here's the plan. \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=309s) So, the AI agent streams a response into our app that is received by the ChatSession class. \[05:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=315s) The ChatSession extracts raw A2UI JSON messages from the agent's responses as it's streaming in and passes them to the A2UI message processor. \[05:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=324s) The message processor is configured with a parser that converts those raw JSON messages into a semantic representation. \[05:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=331s) The processor then validates the messages against the catalog definition and maps them to a set of surface models. \[05:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=338s) The surface models, these are the things that define, how the UI looks and, the pieces of UI that the agent controls. \[05:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=346s) Those surface models are then rendered as native Compose UI using the A2UI surface composable provided by our library. \[05:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=353s) The communication between the agent and the UI is bidirectional, so when the user interacts with the UI, the user actions and errors flow entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/mastering-on-device-intelligence-with-ml-kit-and-litert-in-google-play-services.txt" target="_blank">Mastering on-device intelligence with ML Kit and LiteRT in Google Play services - Speakers: Chintan Parikh (Lead Product Manager), Fergus Henderson (Staff Software Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LiBWWJ9IKag - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/mastering-on-device-intelligence-with-ml-kit-and-litert-in-google-play-services ## About the talk Stop choosing between plug-and-play AI convenience and custom model flexibility---you can deploy both in a single, ultra-lean app without adding megabytes of binary bloat. In this session, we'll demonstrate how to build this exact dual-stack architecture in a single Android app. You'll see how to leverage ML Kit for ready-to-use classical ML tasks (like doc scan) alongside LiteRT standalone in Play services for your custom computer vision or audio workloads. We'll dive deep into how both implementation paths unite under the hood to utilize the modern LiteRT runtime, giving your app seamless, hardware-accelerated performance on CPU and GPUs with a virtually zero-byte download footprint. Key takeaways for developers: -Uncompromised performance: Both turnkey and custom models are hardware-accelerated automatically using the unified CompiledModel API. -Micro-APKs: Dramatically reduce your app's download size by offloading both the ML Kit and LiteRT runtimes to Play services. -Hybrid integration: Master running multiple ML workflows side-by-side in production without resource conflicts. ## Summary - LiteRT in Google Play services shares one maintained runtime across apps to reduce APK sizes by about 8 MB. - Turnkey ML Kit features and custom LiteRT models can run together in a single application on the same runtime. - The CompiledModel API simplifies GPU acceleration and delivers up to 1.4x faster performance than legacy TFLite GPU inference. - Platform availability extends beyond phones to Wear OS 4 or later and Android Automotive OS on Android 11 or later. - Adopting LiteRT in Google Play services involves updating Maven dependencies to \`play-services-litert\`, calling \`LiteRt.initialize\` to obtain an environment, and passing it to \`CompiledModel.create\`. - Migrating to the 2.x CompiledModel API is recommended because 1.x is in maintenance mode and NNAPI is going away. ## Skills - \[Android LiteRT skill\](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/device-ai/litert/) ## Resources - \[Docs \& samples\](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert/android) ## Topics on-device-ai, ml-kit, litert, google-play-services, gpu-acceleration, machine-learning ## Transcript ### Introduction and entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/memory-troubleshooting-with-firebase-crashlytics.txt" target="_blank">Memory troubleshooting with Firebase Crashlytics - Speakers: Polina Govorkova (Senior Software Developer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2ruqmicLr08 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/memory-troubleshooting-with-firebase-crashlytics ## About the talk Keep your app's memory footprint lean-and-mean and non-segfaulty with Firebase Crashlytics. This session explores our comprehensive suite of memory troubleshooting tools available in the Firebase console and in Android Studio. We'll start by covering how to leverage ANR insights and GWP-ASan reports to diagnose elusive memory bugs and then dive into our latest tooling for Out-Of-Memory (OOM) and Memory Limiter Kill (MLK) events, designed specifically to help you navigate and adapt to the new memory limits introduced in Android 17. ## Summary - Application Not Responding errors often trace back to background bottlenecks or memory exhaustion rather than active CPU load. Firebase Crashlytics queries \`ApplicationExitInfo\` to surface multithread traces and identify root blocking threads. - Out of memory crashes occur when apps exceed runtime Java heap limits. Crashlytics integrates with Android 17's \`ProfilingManager\` to collect de-obfuscated heap snapshots that can be inspected in Perfetto or through the Android CLI. - Android 17's Memory Limiter terminates individual processes that consume excessive total RAM, including native allocations. Crashlytics groups these terminations on the dashboard alongside heap dumps to help separate C++ memory leaks from managed heap allocations. - Native memory corruption frequently surfaces on system threads rather than in app code. Crashlytics supports GWP-ASan and Arm MTE, and GWP-ASan reports pinpoint exact allocation and deallocation sites for bugs such as use-after-free. ## Resources - \[ApplicationExitInfo API reference\](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/app/ApplicationExitInfo) - \[ProfilingManager API reference\](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/os/ProfilingManager) - \[Memory Limiter documentation\](https://source.android.com/docs/core/perf/memory-limiter) - \[GWP-ASan guide\](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/gwp-asan) - \[ARM MTE entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/migrating-two-decades-of-the-google-play-app-to-jetpack-compose.txt" target="_blank">Migrating two decades of the Google Play app to Jetpack Compose - Speakers: Kirill Grouchnikov (Software engineer), Jon Boekenoogen (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/migrating-two-decades-of-the-google-play-app-to-jetpack-compose ## About the talk This year, Android officially became Compose-first for building all UI, placing legacy Views into maintenance mode. For Google Play, that journey began back in 2020. Across an engineering footprint spanning nearly two decades and billions of users, migrating to Jetpack Compose was achieved through proven best practices, close collaboration with the core Compose team and continuous tooling evolution. Discover how modernizing Google Play with Compose delivered measurable improvements in velocity and long-term stability. The session walks through connecting agentic Figma design workflows with Compose implementation, automating quality to prevent unnecessary recompositions and crafting expressive interfaces with dynamic color, rich typography and layered shapes. You will leave with tested strategies to triage bugs faster and scale your own Compose migration with confidence. ## Summary - Google Play moved 97% of user impressions to Compose-only screens over six years. Major pages also saw a 30% improvement in jank rate over the past 14 months. - Incremental adoption mitigates business risks across large codebases. Teams can build familiarity on low-traffic screens first, then advance toward hosting \`ComposeView\` directly at the Activity root. - Dynamic theming works entirely in code using \`MaterialTheme\` overlays and the Material Color Utilities library. This avoids Activity teardowns, though generating color schemes at build time helps limit runtime latency. - Unidirectional data flow and declarative UI simplify architecture and remove several types of race conditions. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/moving-beyond-2d-with-custom-3d-geometry-in-the-jetpack-xr-sdk.txt" target="_blank">Moving beyond 2D with custom 3D geometry in the Jetpack XR SDK - Speakers: Egor Yusov (Software Engineer), Jay Abi-Saad (Software Engineer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/moving-beyond-2d-with-custom-3d-geometry-in-the-jetpack-xr-sdk ## About the talk Transitioning your Android applications from traditional 2D screens into spatial environments requires a new approach to constructing shapes. In this session, we will explore the Custom Mesh API in the Jetpack XR SDK, which allows you to programmatically generate procedural 3D geometry directly at runtime. We will walk through the core workflow, from defining vertex layouts to rendering dynamic objects seamlessly within the user's physical space. By the end of this talk, you will have the practical skills to build interactive, custom 3D geometry completely from code. ## Summary - The glTF introspection API in Jetpack SceneCore exposes model metadata at run time. You can play embedded animations, transform subnodes, or override meshes with materials and textures. - Jetpack SceneCore includes mesh APIs to generate custom 3D geometry in Kotlin. Four building blocks such as VertexLayout and \`MeshBuffer\` construct models triangle by triangle without 3D tools. - Dynamic meshes support real-time updates as users draw paths or animate surfaces. Updating only the changed vertex data streams modifications straight to the GPU without recreating the mesh or entity. - Gemini in Android Studio can write complex vertex animation and lighting math for the mesh APIs. One prompt generates working code that animates vertex grids and recalculates normals every frame. ## Resources - \[Android XR Emulator\](https://goo.gle/xr-tools) - \[Jetpack XR SDK\](https://goo.gle/jetpack-xr-sdk) ## Topics jetpack-xr, jetpack-scenecore, android-xr, 3d-geometry, mesh-api, gltf ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android XR and SceneCore \[03:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=225s) Now, Egor will dive deeper into meshes in a moment. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=228s) But for now, let's style up our car. \[03:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=231s) Using our texture API, we can load a PNG image texture, say of a metal pattern. \`\`\`kotlin // Load a PNG with the Texture API val metal = Texture.create( session, Paths.get("textures", "metal.png")) // Create KhronosPbrMaterials val (body, doors, hood) = List(3) { KhronosPbrMaterial .create(session, AlphaMode.OPAQUE) } body.setBaseColorFactor(CYAN) doors.setBaseColorFactor(PINK) hood.setBaseColorTexture(metal) // Override meshes by sub node name val nodes = carEntity.nodes.associateBy { it.name } nodes\["mainBody_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(body) nodes\["lf_door_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(doors) nodes\["rt_door_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(doors) nodes\["hood_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(hood) \`\`\` \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=237s) Then, with our material API, we can plug it right into a \`KhronosPbrMaterial\`. \[04:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=242s) Now, if you're new to 3D, you can think of a mesh as a tabletop, a material as a tablecloth, and a texture as a pattern printed on that cloth. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=252s) But here, instead of a tabletop, we use the material objects we created to override the meshes associated with the car's hood and doors subnodes. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=261s) In just a few lines of code, we've transformed the look and feel of our car, again, all at run time. \[04:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=267s) That's some cool stuff, but here's an even better idea. \[04:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=271s) How awesome would it be to draw a race track for the car to drive on? \[04:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=275s) Here, a pre-made glTF model is not the right fit. \[04:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=279s) Instead, we need the ability to generate 3D geometry on the fly. \[04:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=283s) So, I'll hand it over to Egor to tell you all about our brand-new Jetpack SceneCore mesh APIs. ### Introduction to mesh APIs \[04:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=290s) Thanks, Jay. \[04:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=291s) Let's make it so that the user can draw their race track in the-- with their finger in their living room. \[04:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=297s) The track does not exist until it's drawn, so nobody can model it ahead of time. \[05:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=301s) We will build it in code, one triangle at a time. \[05:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=305s) A mesh starts with vertices, points in space. \`\`\`kotlin // 4 vertices: x, y, z val positions = floatArrayOf( 0f, 0f, 0f, // v0 1f, 0f, 0f, // v1 0f, 1f, 0f, // v2 1f, 1f, 0f // v3 ) // 2 triangles = 6 indices val indices = intArrayOf( 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3 ) \`\`\` \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=309s) Each one carries attributes like a position, a normal for lighting, color, texture coordinates. \[05:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=315s) Indices connect the dots. \[05:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=317s) Every three make a triangle. \[05:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=319s) Two triangles make a square, six indices, but only four vertices, because they share two. \[05:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=326s) Keep going and you get a cube. \[05:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=328s) Every 3D model, including Jay's car, is built the same way, just with more triangles. ### Building blocks of the mesh API \[05:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=335s) Mesh API maps onto that with four building blocks: \`VertexLayout\`, \`MeshBuffer\`, \`CustomMesh\`, and \`MeshEntity\`. \[05:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=342s) Let's take them one at a time. \[05:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=345s) First, VertexLayout. \`\`\`kotlin // How to read each vertex from bytes val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) // 12 B .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) // 12 B .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) // 8 B .build() // stride: 32 B // Offsets and stride are computed, // or set them explicitly. // Attributes can live in separate buffers val split = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .startNextBuffer() .addAttribute(COLOR, UBYTE4_NORM) .build() \`\`\` \[05:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=347s) Your vertex data is just bytes in a ByteBuffer, and every mesh packs them differently. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=350s) VertexLayout says how to read yours: which attributes, what type, and where each one sits. \[05:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=358s) Here, it's a position, a normal, and UVs, the texture coordinates, 32 bytes total. \[06:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=364s) Attributes can also live in separate buffers, so that you can update only the ones that change. \[06:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=370s) Second, \`MeshBuffer\`, a container for raw data. \`\`\`kotlin // Vertex bytes + 32-bit indices val meshBuffer = MeshBuffer.create( session, layout, vertexData = listOf(ByteBufferRegion( vertexBytes, 0, vertexBytes.capacity())), indexData = ByteBufferRegion( indexBytes, 0, indexBytes.capacity())) // Copied to the GPU: reuse your // ByteBuffers right away // Need updates at runtime? val dynamic = MeshBuffer.createDynamic( session, layout, vertexCount = 1000, indexCount = 3000) \`\`\` \[06:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=374s) You give it the layout, the vertex bytes, and 32-bit indices. \[06:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=378s) The data is copied to the GPU right away, so that you can reuse or release your ByteBuffers. \[06:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=384s) By default, the \`MeshBuffer\` is static. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=386s) It's set once and optimized for fast rendering. \[06:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=389s) And if you need to change it at runtime, \`createDynamic\` allocates a fixed capacity that you may update later. \[06:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=397s) Third, \`CustomMesh\`, a view into a \`MeshBuffer\`. \`\`\`kotlin // A view: which indices to draw, and how val road = CustomMesh .BuilderFromMeshBuffer(session, meshBuffer) // subset 0: asphalt .addSubset(TRIANGLES, indexOffset = 0, indexCount = roadCount) // subset 1: lane markings .addSubset(TRIANGLES, indexOffset = roadCount, indexCount = lineCount) .build() // Shortcut: builds MeshBuffer + CustomMesh CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData(session, layout) \`\`\` \[06:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=401s) It doesn't copy any data. \[06:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=403s) It says which range of indices to draw and how, triangles or triangle strips. \[06:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=409s) Here, the asphalt and the lane markings live in the same \`MeshBuffer\`. \[06:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=414s) Multiple custom meshes may share the same \`MeshBuffer\`, and when you don't need sharing, \`BuilderFromMeshData\` creates the mesh and the buffer in one step. \[07:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=424s) Finally, MeshEntity places the mesh in the scene. \`\`\`kotlin // Place the mesh in the scene graph val roadEntity = MeshEntity.create( session, mesh = road, // one material per subset materials = listOf(asphalt, paint), pose = Pose(Vector3(0f, 0f, -1f)), parent = session.scene.activitySpace) // It's an Entity: move it, re-parent it roadEntity.setPose(Pose(Vector3(0f, -0.5f, -1f))) roadEntity.parent = tableAnchor // Same mesh, another entity val ghost = MeshEntity.create( session, road, listOf(glass, glass)) \`\`\` \[07:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=428s) The mesh is the what. \[07:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=430s) The entity is the where. \[07:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=432s) Like the panel and Jay's car, it's an entity, so it has a position and a parent, the thing it is attached to. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=438s) Move the parent, and the road moves with it. \[07:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=441s) You also provide one material per subset, so that the same mesh may appear with different material in different entities. ### Building custom and dynamic meshes \[07:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=451s) So, now let's put it all together and build the mesh, the road mesh. \`\`\`kotlin // Describe a vertex val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) .build() // Path points -\> ribbon of triangles val (vertices, indices) = buildRoad(path) // Build the mesh... val roadMesh = CustomMesh .BuilderFromMeshData(session, layout) .addVertexData(vertices) .setIndexData(indices) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) .build() // ...and put it in the scene val road = MeshEntity.create( session, roadMesh, listOf(asphalt), parent = session.scene.activitySpace) \`\`\` \[07:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=455s) We define the vertex: the position, the normal, and UVs, the texture coordinates. \[07:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=460s) A small helper function turns user path into a ribbon. \[07:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=465s) For each point on the path, it adds two vertices on each side and two triangles that connect them to the next pair. \[07:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=472s) It's plain Kotlin, writing bytes into a ByteBuffer. \[07:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=474s) You don't need any kind of 3D tool. \[08:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=480s) \`BuilderFromMeshData\`, the shortcut we just saw, creates the mesh and the \`MeshBuffer\`, and computes the bounds for us. \[08:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=488s) Finally, \`MeshEntity.create\` places the \`roadMesh\` in the scene with the asphalt material. \[08:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=494s) But we want our track to grow live as the user draws that. \[08:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=498s) For that, we use a dynamic mesh. \`\`\`kotlin // Fixed GPU capacity, allocated once val track = CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData( session, layout, maxVertices = 2 \* MAX_POINTS, maxIndices = 6 \* MAX_POINTS) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) // Covers everything the track can become .setBounds(playArea) .build() // Hand moved: upload only the new segment val buffer = track.meshBuffer buffer.updateVertexData( bufferIndex = 0, vertexData = segmentVertices, offsetInBytes = n \* VERTEX_BYTES) buffer.updateIndexData( segmentIndices, offsetInBytes = n \* INDEX_BYTES) \`\`\` \[08:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=501s) The only difference, we give the builder the maximum capacity up front, so that the GPU buffers can be allocated. \[08:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=508s) Then, as the user draws, \`updateVertexData\` and \`updateIndexData\` upload only the new segments, not the entire mesh. \[08:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=517s) One gotcha: the renderer uses bounds to skip anything off-screen, so set the bounds to cover everything the track may become, like the play area here. \[08:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=528s) You may notice that the API is not the difficult part here. \[08:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=531s) The difficult part is the vertex math, the normals, texture coordinates, triangle order. \[08:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=537s) That's exactly the kind of code that AI is great at writing. \[09:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=541s) But let's say we want to put things one step farther. \[09:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=543s) Now Now, I want a checkered flag waving at the wind at the destination. ### Generating animated meshes with Gemini \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=549s) Vertex animation math is the tricky part, so I asked Gemini. \[09:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=553s) In Android Studio, I gave it one prompt: "Using the Jetpack SceneCore Mesh API, build a 20x12 flag grid with checkerboard UVs, animate a wind wave every frame with updateVertexData, and recompute normals so that the lighting follows the folds." \[09:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=568s) A few seconds later, I got working code. \[09:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=571s) Let's look at what it did. \[09:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=574s) It built a flag mesh as the grid of 20 by 12 cells, two triangles per cell, and it made a smart choice with the layout. \`\`\`kotlin // 20 x 12 cells = 273 vertices val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() // buffer 0: updated every frame .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) .startNextBuffer() // buffer 1: never changes .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) .build() val flagMesh = CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData( session, layout, maxVertices = 273, maxIndices = 1440) .addVertexData(restPose) // buffer 0 .addVertexData(checkerUVs) // buffer 1 .setIndexData(gridIndices) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) .setBounds(swingBounds) .build() \`\`\` \[09:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=581s) Positions and normals are placed in Buffer 0, and they updated every frame. \[09:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=586s) Texture coordinates are placed in Buffer 1, and they never change. \[09:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=590s) The mesh is dynamic, and the bounds are set to cover the full swing of the flag. \[09:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=596s) Every frame, each vertex gets a sine wave that grows towards the free edge, so that the pole side stays put. \`\`\`kotlin // Gemini wrote the math fun wave(t: Float) { for (i in 0 until 273) { val u = (i % 21) / 20f // 0 at the pole setZ(i, 0.06f \* u \* sin(6f \* u - 4f \* t)) } recomputeNormals() // from neighbors } // Every frame: one upload (\~6.5 KB) while (isActive) withFrameNanos { ns -\> wave(ns / 1e9f) flagMesh.meshBuffer.updateVertexData( bufferIndex = 0, vertexData = ByteBufferRegion( posNormals, 0, 273 \* 24)) } \`\`\` \[10:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=605s) The normals are recomputed from the neighboring positions, which is what makes the folds catch the light. \[10:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=610s) \`updateVertexData\` uploads about 6.5 KB of data to the GPU each frame. \[10:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=616s) We do not recreate the mesh or the entity. \[10:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=619s) Now let's see it all together. \[10:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=621s) We place the car model on the table, then we use ARCore to draw the track. \[10:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=627s) The mesh flag we just-- the flag mesh we just built appears at the destination. \[10:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=632s) The car drives along the track, and we use glTF Introspection API to steer and spin the wheels of the car. \[10:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=639s) The mesh appears with the asphalt material, but we can also use mesh API together with the material API to change the look and feel of the road, like you can see on the video. \[10:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=648s) That is like that is some powerful stuff right at your finger fingertips. ### Summary and getting started \[10:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=654s) Today, we've covered a lot of ways to take your apps from 2D to spatial. \[10:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=659s) With the glTF Introspection API, you can now tap directly into the inner metadata of a glTF model, triggering embedded animations, transforming individual subnodes, and even swapping materials to alter its look and feel all at runtime. \[11:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=673s) Then, we saw that when pre-made 3D models weren't enough, we could leverage our brand new Mesh API to build custom geometry. \[11:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=681s) Whether you need to build static shapes from scratch or stream dynamic shapes dynamic geometry in real time, you now have the tools to do so. \[11:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=689s) And like Egor just showed, pairing those building blocks with Gemini means you don't even need to do the math alone. \[11:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=695s) Now, I'll repeat something I said earlier: everything you saw was running in an Android app, written in idiomatic Kotlin, right inside Android Studio. \[11:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=704s) I see a lot of laptops in the audience today, and I hope that Egor and I excited you enough to open up Android Studio and spin up the Android XR Emulator today. \[11:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=713s) Let your imagination run loose, and use your existing Android skills, along with what we showed today, to build amazing XR experiences. \[12:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=721s) On behalf of Egor and myself, thank you so much for joining us today, and enjoy the rest of the Android Dev Summit.</a>

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/navigating-multi-device-quality-publishing-beyond-mobile-on-google-play.txt" target="_blank">Navigating multi-device quality \& publishing beyond mobile on Google Play - Speakers: Jan Kleinert (Developer Relations Engineer), Faustine Liao (DFX Operations Lead) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/navigating-multi-device-quality-publishing-beyond-mobile-on-google-play ## About the talk As the Android ecosystem expands across wrists, living rooms, vehicles, and XR, the opportunity to reach users on new screens is growing. However, distributing across Wear OS, Android TV, Android Auto, Android Automotive OS, or Android XR introduces distinct considerations for testing, store listings, and app reviews. This session explores how to effectively utilize Google Play Console for non-mobile form factors to help streamline a predictable multi-device launch. We will cover key distribution decisions, including how to structure track strategies and package names, configure targeted testing tracks, and tailor store listings. You'll get a practical walkthrough of form-factor App Quality guidelines to help avoid common review pitfalls and publish on Google Play with greater confidence. ## Summary - Modular app bundles isolate form-factor releases from your mobile app. If a form-factor review fails, only that specific bundle is blocked while your mobile release publishes as intended. - Play Console tracks offer flexible publishing paths, with exceptions for Wear OS and Android Auto. Wear OS requires a dedicated track, while Android Auto must use the standard mobile track. - Internal testing tracks distribute builds to up to 100 testers without triggering a Play review. Closed and open testing tracks do trigger reviews, helping you resolve hurdles before launch. - Form-factor review rejections often stem from missed device requirements, such as car app category limits or absent screenshots. Provide valid demo account credentials in Play Console whenever your app requires login. ## Resources - \[Android user experience guidelines\](https://developer.android.com/quality/user-experience) - \[Android TV app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/tv-app-quality) - \[Android XR app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/xr-app-quality) - \[Android for Cars app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/car-app-quality) - \[Wear OS app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/wear-app-quality) ## Topics google-play, multi-device, android-tv, android-auto, wear-os, android-xr, app-quality ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=5s) Welcome, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=6s) Thank you so much for joining us for this session on navigating multi-device app quality and publishing on Google Play for form factors beyond mobile. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=14s) I'm Jan Kleinert, a Developer Relations Engineer on the Android for Cars team. \[00:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=18s) And I'm Faustine Liao, an Operations Lead on the Play Trust and Safety team. \[00:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=22s) We are so excited to have everyone here with us today. \[00:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=25s) So for years, when we said Android development, most of us really pictured just like a mobile device, but the Android ecosystem has expanded far beyond just smartphones. \[00:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=34s) So today, your users are interacting with apps in their living rooms on Android TV, maybe in the carpool line or while they're charging their cars on Android Auto or Automotive OS, on their wrists with Wear OS, and increasingly in immersive 3D spaces with Android XR. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=52s) This is a massive opportunity for growth, but expanding to these form factors means there are just a few marginal considerations to take into account for your publishing strategy. \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=61s) The overall process from building your app to having it published and live on Google Play remains generally the same as you're used to for mobile releases. \[01:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=70s) Build and prepare your app, then create your listing in Play Console, test your app, upload and submit your production release, and then wait for review and approval. \[01:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=80s) However, there are some unique considerations for publishing apps for form factors beyond mobile. \[01:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=86s) And today, we're going to give you a clear framework to help you prepare for a smoother, more predictable multi-device release process. \[01:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=94s) Let's start with the foundation: how to architect and package your app. ### App architecture and packaging \[01:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=100s) So before you even touch Google Play Console, you have an important architectural decision to make. Internal testing shows a 2x speedup compared to running models in the cloud. - Gemini Nano memory usage dropped from 3.6 GB to 1.1 GB. Key optimizations include 2-bit quantization and a shared KV cache. - Prefix caching and speculative decoding significantly accelerate inference. Reusing system prompts cuts processed tokens by 60%, while a smaller drafter model delivers an average 2x speedup. - New on-device capabilities expand app interactions through speech translation and function calling. Adding thinking mode raises tool-calling accuracy on Gemini Nano 4 by 13 points out of 100. - Multimodal embeddings combine with AppSearch to store and retrieve data through cosine similarity. Your app executes the search logic locally, protecting user privacy and data security. ## Resources - \[Prompt API Android documentation\](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/genai/prompt/android) ## entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/optimize-media-playback-and-maximize-reach-with-jetpack-media3-apis.txt" target="_blank">Optimize media playback and maximize reach with Jetpack Media3 APIs - Speakers: Donovan McMurray (Developer Relations Engineer), Toni Heidenreich (Software Engineer), Kristina Simakova (Engineering Manager) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/optimize-media-playback-and-maximize-reach-with-jetpack-media3-apis ## About the talk Media consumption accounts for a large portion of user time spent on mobile devices, which requires the playback experience to be flawless, highly efficient and mindful of battery life. Furthermore, users expect these experiences to seamlessly transition across their devices, from phones to living room TVs and beyond. Explore how architectural updates in Media3 and ExoPlayer power seamless playback across form factors. The discussion centers on crafting responsive interfaces with the Media3 Compose UI toolkit, eliminating buffering in feeds using the new PreloadManager and extending your app to living room screens and Android XR with CastPlayer and spatial audio. ## Summary - Media3 UI Compose provides ready-made player composables and customizable building blocks. You can override specific control slots while letting the library manage player state and transitions. - A newly rewritten CastPlayer replaces the standalone Cast SDK. It implements the standard player interface and automatically delegates playback between local ExoPlayer instances and remote Cast devices. - The rebuilt editing pipeline decouples from OpenGL and manages hardware buffers directly. This zero-copy approach lowers memory overhead, and decoupling lets developers integrate modern graphic frameworks like WebGPU. - Media3 adds out-of-the-box support for Eclipsa Video and Eclipsa Audio on Android 17 and later. Prescriptive HDR metadata adapts highlights to ambient light, while spatial audio handles multiple mixed presentations. - Built-in optimizations like PCM audio offload reduce screen-off power consumption by up to 20%. The upcoming CodecDB uses benchmark metrics to select device-optimal encoder settings. ## Resources - \[Media3 GitHub repository\](https://github.com/androidx/media) - \[Media3 developer documentation\](https://goo.gle/media3) ## Topics jetpack-media3, exoplayer, jetpack-compose, google-cast, video-editing, audio, performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to Jetpack Media3 entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/outperform-yourself-in-compose.txt" target="_blank">Outperform yourself in Compose - Speakers: Andrei Shikov (Software Engineer), Andrew Bailey (Software Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t5ujT_o8qj0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/outperform-yourself-in-compose ## About the talk Jetpack Compose makes it easy to design high-quality user interfaces, but it can be difficult to track down issues that affect UI performance. These kinds of issues can lead to problems that your users notice, like startup latency, and dropped frames that appear as scroll jank or choppy animations. In this talk, we'll introduce tools to uncover what's impacting your UI's performance, focusing on Perfetto and (re-)composition tracing. We'll then explore specific anti-patterns you may be using that are secretly costing you, how you can find them in your code, and what positive patterns you can replace them with. By the end of this talk, you'll understand how to think in Compose with a performance mindset, and how to profile, analyze, and verify performance optimizations in your app. ## Summary - Perfetto traces record on-device activity and show Compose slices such as composition and layout along the main thread. Use them to inspect frame timelines and track phase durations. - Every operation inside composables has a cost, including launching and canceling coroutines. Audit side effect APIs and consider merging effects with identical keys to reduce composition overhead. - Composition tracing annotates composable functions, and recomposition tracing (1.13+) tracks state reads and writes causing recomposition. They help diagnose unexpected work directly within Perfetto traces. - ComputedState (Compose 1.13+) avoids unwanted invalidations and is typically faster than DerivedState during read-after-write invalidations. DerivedState remains useful when expensive calculations or allocations benefit from caching. - Skipping composables carries upkeep costs and parameter comparison overhead. Rely on strong skipping and object identity equality, or avoid invalidations entirely, rather than forcing stability. ## Skills - \[Android Skills repository\](https://github.com/android/skills) ## Resources - \[Perfetto Trace Viewer\](https://ui.perfetto.dev) - \[Composition and recomposition tracing guide\](https://goo.gle/composition-tracing) - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Optimizing with LLMs and Android Skills\](https://developer.android.com/tools/agents/android-skills) ## Topics jetpack-compose, android-performance, perfetto, benchmarking, coroutines, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/powering-interactive-surfaces-with-remote-compose.txt" target="_blank">Powering interactive surfaces with Remote Compose - Speakers: Nicolas Roard (Sr Staff Software Engineer), John Hoford (Developer), John Zoeller (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=csh2Opo_wjE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/powering-interactive-surfaces-with-remote-compose ## About the talk Remote Compose introduces a new way to project expressive and interactive UI onto remote surfaces like widgets. By serializing layouts into compact binary payloads, RemoteCompose decouples UI from host execution to deliver significant advantages. Key benefits include edge interactivity that enables high-performance rendering through local execution on the remote device, fluid scaling that allows UIs to reflow across diverse form factors via remote-side component evaluations, and a unified developer workflow that removes the need for platform-specific remote UI frameworks through familiar Jetpack Compose APIs. This session unpacks these benefits and provides live production examples, including modern Wear OS Widgets and the glanceable Wear Workout Tracker experience in Runkeeper. ## Summary - Remote Compose packages UI into a compact binary document instead of sending an app or screen copy across process boundaries. - Developers create documents using Compose APIs or JSON. Android Studio provides live previews while writing composables. - Loaded documents run by themselves directly on the player. They handle events such as resizing and touch without round trips to its creator. - Built-in optimizations such as component templates and document compression shrink payloads down to a few kilobytes. - Jetpack Glance emits Remote Compose documents for launcher widgets and Wear OS widgets. This decouples the UI from app execution to save battery. ## Resources - \[ASICS Runkeeper Wear OS open beta\](https://goo.gle/runkeeper-wearos) - \[Migrating Wear OS tiles to widgets\](https://goo.gle/wearos-tiles-widgets-migration) ## Topics remote-compose, jetpack-compose, android-widgets, wear-os, ui-framework ## Transcript ### Introduction and overview of Remote entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scale-your-app-for-every-screen-with-compose.txt" target="_blank">Scale your app for every screen with Compose - Speakers: Francesco Romano (Senior Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scale-your-app-for-every-screen-with-compose ## About the talk The Android ecosystem is vast, with users shifting seamlessly across phones, tablets, foldables, and desktop environments. Now that we are Compose First, this session explores how to architect your app for resizable windows and diverse aspect ratios---where traditional layout assumptions break down, leading to stretched UIs and lost state. Explore how the latest capabilities in Jetpack Compose, Navigation 3, and WindowManager can help you build dynamic layouts that naturally scale from compact screens to dual-pane displays. Walk away with strategies to accelerate your development workflow using Gemini and our skills, like the adaptive skill, to automatically refactor legacy codebases for larger screens. ## Summary - Android platforms require adaptive apps because the system ignores orientation and aspect ratio locks on larger screens starting in Android 16, with manifest opt-outs removed in Android 17. - The experimental \`MediaQuery\` API declaratively tracks active UI capabilities such as window size and folding postures. It replaces stitching together multiple legacy platform managers into Compose state. - Stable \`Grid\` and \`FlexBox\` primitives provide adaptive layout building blocks. \`Grid\` enables parameterized multi-dimensional arrangements within a single composable, while \`FlexBox\` provides one-dimensional space distribution and wrapping. - Jetpack Navigation 3 structures app-level multi-pane flows around state and scenes. Custom scene strategies evaluate UI capabilities and window size classes to dynamically switch between single-pane and multi-pane presentations. - Compose Adaptive skills for Gemini automate app migrations to modern responsive components. The updated skill refactors layouts, resolves state loss bugs, and configures desktop inputs such as keyboard shortcuts and cursors. ## Resources - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Topics jetpack-compose, adaptive-layouts, mediaquery, grid-layout, flexbox, navigation-3, android-skills ## Transcript ### Introduction to scaling apps across screens \*\*Francesco Romano\*\* entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scaling-input-interactions-beyond-the-touchscreen-with-jetpack-compose.txt" target="_blank">Scaling input interactions beyond the touchscreen with Jetpack Compose - Speakers: Alex Vanyo (Software Engineer), Jeremy Walker (Compose Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iztM_PgoCjw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scaling-input-interactions-beyond-the-touchscreen-with-jetpack-compose ## About the talk As new form factors move beyond the touchscreen, Compose's input system has evolved to meet the challenge. Its layered architecture provides the foundation for supporting everything from advanced trackpad gestures to novel hardware inputs seamlessly. Through clear architectural breakdowns and hands-on code examples, follow the lifecycle of an input event all the way from the OS platform layer up to Compose gesture detectors and UI components. You will discover how to trace events across the entire stack, apply key architectural patterns for emerging input types, and confidently debug complex gesture interactions in your own apps. ## Summary - Jetpack Compose processes incoming Android pointer events through a six-phase pipeline. This pipeline maintains a hit path tree and dispatches events in three passes across UI nodes. - Trackpad inputs in Compose now map to mouse events instead of touch. Compose also converts platform fake finger events into dedicated pan and scale pointer events. - Intelligent eyewear trackpads introduce indirect input types rather than screen coordinate touches. They use a Primary Directional Motion Axis to map horizontal swipes into vertical next or previous navigation. - Testing support has expanded beyond touch with new methods such as \`performTrackpadInput\`. These APIs provide familiar testing surfaces to validate that apps handle non-touch devices correctly. ## Topics jetpack-compose, pointer-input, trackpads, gestures, intelligent-eyewear, accessibility entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/take-compose-state-beyond-the-ui-with-jetpack-appstate.txt" target="_blank">Take Compose state beyond the UI with Jetpack AppState - Speakers: Ben Sagmoe (Developer Relations Engineer), Elif Bilgin Morris (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/take-compose-state-beyond-the-ui-with-jetpack-appstate ## About the talk Compose's snapshot runtime, automatic dependency tracking, and atomic updates don't have to stop at the UI layer. Jetpack AppState lets you move Compose state upstream---streamlining what reaches your screens by hoisting and deriving state with the snapshot system before it ever hits the UI. In this session, you'll learn about AppState's two foundational libraries. We'll dive into StateStore for hoisting state, and Transform for using composition to derive state with plain Kotlin control flow---eliminating complex Flow combine chains and keeping your UI effortlessly in sync. ## Summary - Compose Runtime works as a general-purpose state management engine without Compose UI. Its snapshot system tracks reads dynamically and keeps concurrent updates consistent across properties. - Jetpack AppState Transform computes and exposes Compose State from headless composable blocks. It replaces complex Flow operator chains like \`combine\` while supporting early returns and nested state derivations. - Transform uses an eager headless frame clock to run transformations off the UI thread. The clock parks whenever watched states remain unchanged, avoiding wasted work. - Jetpack AppState StateStore shares Compose State across distinct components like activities and background services. Integrating it with DataStore lets individual keys survive process death without custom boilerplate. ## Resources - \[Molecule library on GitHub\](https://github.com/cashapp/molecule) - \[AppState documentation\](https://goo.gle/appstate-docs) - \[AppState Recipes repository on GitHub\](https://www.github.com/android/appstate-recipes) ## Topics jetpack-compose, jetpack-appstate, state-management, android-architecture, compose-runtime ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=6s) Hello, and welcome to Take Compose State Beyond the UI with Jetpack AppState. \[00:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=10s) My name is Ben, and I am a developer relations engineer working on that Jetpack architecture libraries. \[00:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=15s) And I'm Elif, and I'm one of the engineers who work on the app architecture libraries. \[00:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=19s) And today, we're here to talk to you about a future where Compose goes beyond the UI and into the data and domain layers of applications. \[00:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=27s) So, as I'm sure you're all well aware by now, Compose is the recommended toolkit for UI development on Android. \[00:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=33s) From tat-- phones and tablets to widgets, watches, TVs, and XR devices, Compose powers it all. \[00:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=39s) But as your app grows across these UI surfaces and background components, managing the state behind them gets harder, especially around two common pain points. \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=50s) The first is deriving complex state. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=52s) Weaving together multiple data streams, local UI inputs, and ambient state, like network connectivity, that often turns into a tangle of operators like combine, flatMapLatest, and distinctUntilChanged. \[01:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=64s) And then the second is sharing state across components: keeping an activity, service, app widget, and more in sync, and making sure that that state can survive proc-ground-- process death when needed. \[01:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=76s) When we stepped back to look at these challenges, we came to look at how Compose itself is built. \[01:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=81s) Most people think of Compose as a UI toolkit, but it's actually two distinct layers: Compose UI on top and the Compose Runtime underneath. \[01:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=88s) While Compose UI handles layout, drawing, and input, the Compose Runtime is a general purpose engine for state management and recomposition. \[01:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=96s) It has no dependency on the UI. \[01:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=99s) And that's the realization that led us to build Jetpack AppState. \[01:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=103s) It's a family of libraries focused on making the most of Compose state beyond the UI. ### What is Compose State? \[01:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=109s) But before we dive into AppState, let's make sure we're on the same page when we talk about what we mean by property during the execution of a \[Composable\] \* function, the current \[RecomposeScope\] will be subscribed to changes of that value. \*/ @Stable public interface State { public val value: T } \`\`\` \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=120s) And the interface you're probably more familiar with, \`MutableState\`. \`\`\`kotlin /\*\* \* A mutable value holder where reads to the \[value\] property during the execution of a \[Composable\] \* function, the current \[RecomposeScope\] will be subscribed to changes of that value. When the \* \[value\] property is written to and changed, a recomposition of any subscribed \[RecomposeScope\]s \* will be scheduled. If \[value\] is written to with the same value, no recompositions will be \* scheduled. \*/ @Stable public interface MutableState : State { override var value: T public operator fun component1(): T public operator fun component2(): (T) -\> Unit } \`\`\` \[02:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=124s) Fundamentally, these are just bare-bones containers. routes reads and writes through the snapshot system. \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=143s) And whenever your code runs inside of a snapshot observer, like a composition, you Column { Text("Count: ${count.value}") AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } \`\`\` \[02:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=155s) So, automatic means that there's no subscribing at Counter here, reading \`count.value\` directly inside the composable reports to the that read to the composition, and it registers Counter in its list of readers. \[02:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=172s) And now look at \`AddButton\`. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Column { Text("Count: ${count.value}") AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } @Composable fun AddButton(onClick: () -\> Unit) { Button(onClick = onClick) { Text("Add") } } \`\`\` \[02:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=177s) When a user clicks \`AddButton\` and modifies count, the snapshot system tracks that write, which lets the composition know to invalidate entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/the-car-is-your-canvas-unlocking-android-development-for-the-road.txt" target="_blank">The car is your canvas: Unlocking Android development for the road - Speakers: Paul Lammertsma (Developer Relations Engineer), Thomas Weathers (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8YkU3aPbQYA - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/the-car-is-your-canvas-unlocking-android-development-for-the-road ## About the talk As in-car displays expand across Android Auto and Android Automotive OS vehicles, developers face a unique dual challenge: delivering rich, adaptive experiences while parked, and driver-safe, template-driven experiences while driving. In this comprehensive 30-minute technical session, we explore the end-to-end architecture and development approaches to adapting Android apps to cars. From the fundamentals of designing apps for use in cars, to the newest approaches for building media experiences that shift from audio to video as the car shifts from drive to park, you'll leave with everything you need to know to get your app on the road. ## Summary - Android for Cars targets two platforms: Android Auto and Android Automotive OS. One projects from a phone, while the other runs directly on the vehicle. - The Car App Library provides templates for driving-optimized interfaces that adapt to various car hardware configurations. - Parked car apps rely on standard Android activities for rich experiences like video streaming, games, and web browsers. - Car App Library 1.9 brings new UI components and brand customization tokens. It also expands media template support fully to Android Automotive OS. - Park-to-drive capabilities dynamically launch native video activities when parked, then switch back to media templates to maintain uninterrupted audio when driving. ## Resources - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Android for Cars documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-cars) - \[Build games for cars guide\](https://goo.gle/games-in-cars) - \[What's new in Android for Cars\](https://d.android.com/training/cars/whats-new) ## Topics android-for-cars, android-auto, android-automotive-os, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/trace-me-if-you-can-automated-instrumentation-and-field-profiling.txt" target="_blank">Trace me if you can: Automated instrumentation and field profiling - Speakers: Rahul Ravikumar (Staff Software Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZtQgeIrmAo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/trace-me-if-you-can-automated-instrumentation-and-field-profiling ## About the talk Optimizing Android apps requires deep visibility into concurrent workflows and coroutine suspensions. While local profiling offers a useful snapshot, scaling these insights to production without overhead remains a challenge. This session delivers an architectural blueprint for a continuous performance feedback loop. androidx.tracing 2.0: Swap backends dynamically and propagate coroutine contexts (Perfetto flows) across threads. Smart Instrumentation: Use local ART tracing to find hotspots, then automate the injection of low-overhead trace points. Macrobenchmarking: Track regressions and verify performance gains on physical devices in CI. Field Tracing: Go beyond local and CI tracing, with ProfilingManager. ## Summary - Tracing 2.0 replaces older Android tracing APIs to remove label length limits and run seven times faster. It also lets you build custom sinks for backends such as OpenTelemetry. - Context propagation maps causal relationships across threads, coroutines, and processes. You can track asynchronous execution with \`traceCoroutine\` or pass propagation tokens into callback-based code. - Jetpack Compose 1.13 adds Recomposition Tracing, using custom metadata to show why recompositions occur. Traces record the modified state values and the exact call stacks that triggered them. - Android build tools use Tracing 2.0 to spot bottlenecks and speed up builds. Tracing guided optimizations that made R8 code shrinking 25% faster and cut Metalava post-submit times by 15%. ## Topics tracing, android-performance, perfetto, context-propagation, jetpack-compose, coroutines, profiling ## Transcript ### Introduction \& evolution of Android tracing \*\*Rahul Ravikumar\*\* \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZtQgeIrmAo\&t=7s) Good afternoon, everyone. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/type-safe-keep-rules-and-dex-optimization.txt" target="_blank">Type safe keep rules and DEX optimization - Speakers: Chris Craik (Android Performance Engineer), Breana Tate (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/type-safe-keep-rules-and-dex-optimization ## About the talk Android apps often ship under-optimized due to overly conservative keep rules often from third-party libraries, leading to bloated APKs, slower cold starts, and degraded runtime performance. With Google Play's new performance thresholds for DEX optimization, app visibility now directly depends on staying ahead of the optimization curve. This talk introduces a modern R8 workflow to tackle rule bloat. You will learn to: - Use the R8 config analyzer and skill to identify legacy rule overhead. - Transition from broad wildcard keep rules to precise, type-safe, generated annotations. - Prevent optimization regressions with new Android CLI tools. ## Summary - Google Play enforces app-quality thresholds requiring more than 25% code optimization. Meeting them reduces memory usage while improving start-up speed and ANR rates. - The R8 Configuration Analyzer generates an HTML report showing which keep rules retain code. It highlights subsumed and unused rules and measures optimization potential before compilation. - Overly broad keep rules, often introduced to prevent reflection crashes or inherited from libraries, undermine app optimization. A single package-wide wildcard rule can keep dozens of unused classes. - Jetpack Keep uses lint to detect reflection and generate precise annotations and conditional keep rules directly from code. It exports standard consumer rules compatible with older R8 versions. - Android CLI inspects app bundles and AARs using Google Play's exact logic without an upload. It flags problematic rules and exports JSON reports for automated regression testing. ## Resources - \[App quality memory optimization blog post\](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/08/app-quality-memory-optimization-secure-onboarding.html) - \[Google Play Console\](https://play.google.com/console) - \[R8 analyzer guide\](https://goo.gle/r8-analyzer) - \[Android CLI documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[R8 optimization documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-r8) - \[Jetpack Keep documentation\](https://goo.gle/jetpack-keep) ## Topics dex-optimization, r8, keep-rules, jetpack-keep, android-cli, app-performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to DEX optimization \[00:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs\&t=9s) And I'm Chris Craik, I'm on the Android Performance team. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs\&t=13s) Welcome to type-safe keep rules and DEX optimization. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs\&t=16s) Today, we're going to talk about what DEX optimization is, why you should care, and also, some In this session, we dive into ML Kit's new agentic APIs, built directly on top of the direct model access APIs you already know. Using the open-source Jetpacker app, you'll learn how to chain multi-step actions across local data, manage stateful multi-turn sessions with isolated contexts, and wire up Android MCP to power both in-app assistants and Android system-level surfaces with a single codebase. ## Summary - Gemini Nano 4 natively supports Function Calling, letting on-device models translate natural language into actions and drive local APIs. - The Jetpack AppFunctions library defines tools through natural-language KDoc descriptions. Changing access levels can expose these functions to system agents such as Gemini. - The new agentic flows library (alpha) in ML Kit GenAI simplifies building agents by handling the execution loop and tool calls. - \`AgentRunner\` coordinates tool execution and provides session methods for multi-turn conversations without losing context. - Direct access via the Prompt API remains available for simple history control or complex setups like multi-agent and hybrid systems. ## Skills - \[Android Skills\](https://goo.gle/android-skills) ## Resources - \[Jetpacker sample code\](https://goo.gle/jetpacker) - \[AICore Developer Preview\](https://goo.gle/aicore-dev-preview) ## Topics ml-kit, on-device-ai, gemini-nano, ai-agents, function-calling, app-functions, aicore ## entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/whats-new-in-android-dev-tools.txt" target="_blank">What's new in Android dev tools - Speakers: Esteban de la Canal (Software Engineer), Adarsh Fernando (Group Product Manager) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w-auFZP5gJo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/whats-new-in-android-dev-tools ## About the talk Discover what's next for Android development across Android Studio and the terminal with Android CLI. In this session, we unveil the latest in Android Studio Canary and Stable---from AI-assisted code migrations to Compose and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) support, to Lightbuild's declarative architecture. We'll also dive into the latest updates to the Android CLI toolchain. Learn how you can use it to automate your inner-loop workflows with improved access to devices, diagnostics tools for local and production issues, profiling workflows that let your agents test and validate optimizations and much more. ## Summary - Android CLI provides structured, predictable commands without interactive prompts, built specifically to help modern coding agents navigate developer workflows. - New Android CLI commands let agents render Compose previews without Android Studio and inspect production crashes from Crashlytics. They can also delta-push APK updates during installation. - Native Android x86 APK execution directly on Linux desktops runs apps as single processes with Logcat output and without nested virtualization. - Official Android plugins equip agents in Google Antigravity and Claude Code with Android CLI and architectural guidelines. Antigravity can view Compose previews and interact directly with devices. - Android Studio Rabbit 2 introduces Bring Your Own Agent and AI Change Review to inspect pull requests and fix issues. ## Resources - \[Android Studio download\](https://d.android.com/studio) - \[Android CLI feedback and downloads\](https://d.android.com/cli) ## Topics android-cli, ai-agents, android-studio, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/xr-is-for-everyone-designing-accessible-spatial-experiences.txt" target="_blank">XR is for everyone: Designing accessible spatial experiences - Speakers: Jazmin Cano (User Experience Research Lead) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FCuqj4bwvB4 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/xr-is-for-everyone-designing-accessible-spatial-experiences ## About the talk When we say XR is for everyone, that principle has to guide how we build from day one. In this introductory guide for developers new to XR, Jazmin Cano shares the foundational accessibility principles honed at Owlchemy Labs. Engine-agnostic and universally applicable to both games and apps, this session explores how early consideration of motor, visual, auditory, and cognitive needs leads to better experiences for all users. Discover how to build an inclusive development culture, conduct meaningful testing, and design spatial interactions that remove barriers without sacrificing quality. ## Summary - Spatial interfaces risk excluding users if access needs are omitted during early design. Consider accessibility across physical and cognitive categories from the very start. - Disability affects 1.3 billion people worldwide, including roughly 20% of gamers. Designing for specific access needs often benefits a wider audience in temporary or situational contexts. - Physical accessibility features reduce body strain and accommodate limited mobility. Useful options include scalable environments (such as small human mode) and artificial snap turning. - Vision and auditory aids provide critical cues across alternate senses. Useful implementations include high-contrast object glows and directional subtitles. - Testing with diverse groups helps teams iterate effectively on spatial designs. Involve people across varied disabilities and age groups throughout development. - Developers should prototype inclusively from the beginning, test with diverse users, and make an immediate commitment to implement at least one accessible feature. ## Resources - \[XR Accessibility Project\](https://xraccessibility.github.io/) - \[GAConf\](https://www.gaconf.com/) - \[GAConf Archive\](https://www.gaconf.com/archive/) - \[Owlchemy Labs\](https://OwlchemyLabs.com) - \[Owlchemy Labs Resources and White Papers\](https://www.owlchemylabs.com/resources) ## Topics xr, entries.title: Widget quality
entries.summary: Widgets are a critical component for customizing a user's home screen. Often, users can achieve a critical user journey for an app with a single tap using widgets or get a quick summary of important updates. Users can also customize widgets to tailor them to individual preferences.

entries.title: Keep the screen on
entries.summary: Certain apps need to keep the screen turned on, such as games or movie apps. Some Android APIs automatically keep the screen on for you. In other cases, you can set a flag to manually keep the screen on.

entries.title: System restrictions on background tasks
entries.summary: Background processes can be memory- and battery-intensive. For example, an implicit broadcast may start many background processes that have registered to listen for it, even if those processes may not do much work. This can have a substantial impact on both device performance and user experience.

entries.title: Stability in Compose
entries.summary: Compose considers types to be either stable or unstable. A type is stable if it is immutable, or if it is possible for Compose to know whether its value has changed between recompositions. A type is unstable if Compose can't know whether its value has changed between recompositions.
